Appeal from the United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio at Toledo. 
No. 3:19-cv-02854—James R. Knepp II, District Judge. 

Argued: October 20, 2026 
Decided and Filed: November 2, 2026 
Before: GIBBONS, SUTTON, and DAVIS, Circuit Judges. 
_________________ 
COUNSEL 
ARGUED: Matthew I. Henzi, ASHERKELLY LAW, PLLC, Southfield, Michigan, for 
Appellant. Daniel F. Gourash, SEELEY SAVIDGE EBERT & GOURASH CO., LLP, 
Westlake, Ohio, for Appellee s Everest Indemnity Insurance Company and EverSports 
& Entertainment Insurance, Inc. R. Christopher Yingling, NICOLA, GUDBRANSON & 
COOPER, LLC, Cleveland, Ohio, for Appellee Bearing Insurance Group. ON BRIEF : 
Matthew I. Henzi, ASHERKELLY LAW, PLLC, Southfield, Michigan, for Appellant. Daniel F. 
Gourash, Robert D. Anderle, Clare C. Moran, SEELEY SAVIDGE EBERT & GOURASH CO., 
LLP, Westlake, Ohio, for Appellee s Everest Indemnity Insurance Company and EverSports 
& Entertainment Insurance, Inc. R. Christopher Yingling, NICOLA, GUDBRANSON & 
COOPER, LLC, Cleveland, Ohio, for Appellee Bearing Insurance Group, LLC. 
> 
No. 25-4018 Sinmier, LLC v. Everest Indemnity Ins. Co., et al. Page 2 

_________________ 
OPINION 
_________________ 
SUTTON, Circuit Judge. Sinmier, a commercial real estate lender, loaned Vintro Hotels 
and Resorts funds to purchase a resort in Sandusky, Ohio, and recorded a mortgage as security. 
When Vintro defaulted on its obligation, Sinmier discovered that the resort’s insurance policies 
left its mortgagee interest unprotected. Vintro and Sinmier executed a settlement agreement that 
released Vintro’s mortgage debt and transferred a deed in lieu of foreclosure to Maui Sands in 
Sinmier’s name. Because Sinmier still had not recovered all of its original investment, it brought 
this action in its capacity as mortgagee against Vintro’s insurance broker, one of Vintro’s 
insurance providers, and an underwriter. The district court granted summary judgment to the 
defendants. Seeing no error, we affirm. 
I. 
Sinmier is a commercial real estate lender. In 2018, it loaned Vintro Hotels and Resorts, 
a hotel operator, seven million dollars to purchase the Maui Sands Resort and Waterpark in 
Sandusky, Ohio, via an Open -End Mortgage and Security Agreement. Sinmier recorded a 
mortgage on September 7, 2018. 
Obligated by contract to insure the property, Vintro used Bankers, an insurance broker, to 
identify various avenues of coverage. Bankers contacted a wholesale insurance broker to seek 
quotes on Vintro’s behalf. Two insurance companies, Everest and Berkley, entered the picture. 
Both insurance companies eventually proposed policies. 
On August 23, 2018, Berkley issued a policy, but it soon cancelled the policy when 
Vintro did not make a down payment at the proposed closing. Everest likewise issued a policy 
effective August 23, 2018. When the closing failed to occur on time, Everest also cancelled its 
policy and told the wholesale broker it would have to re-write the policy. 
 On October 16, Bankers asked the wholesale broker to obtain a revised policy quote with 
an effective date of October 19, 2018. Everest issued a second policy, but it listed Sinmier only 
No. 25-4018 Sinmier, LLC v. Everest Indemnity Ins. Co., et al. Page 3 

as an additional insured, not as a mortgagee, under the commercial general liability portion of the 
agreement. This time around, the closing of the sale of Maui Sands occurred as planned. 
 Then came a rough Ohio winter. Located on Lake Erie, Maui Sands suffered. A frozen 
pipe burst and caused major flooding. Two HVAC systems located on the roof froze, and then 
(surprisingly) caught fire, leaving a smoky, humid waterpark. Still more wind -generated and 
cold-related losses mounted at Maui Sands. 
On January 26, 2019, Vintro submitted an insurance claim to Everest. The insurance 
company advanced $350,000 to Vintro while it processed the claim. Vintro and Everest 
ultimately settled Vintro’s policy claim for an additional $775,000 in June 2019. 
 In March 2019, after Vintro defaulted on its loan obligation, Sinmier sued Vintro. See 
Complaint at 3–7, Sinmier, LLC v. Vintro Hotels & Resorts Ohio LLC , No. 19 -cv-705 (N.D. 
Ohio Mar. 29, 2019). Sinmier sought relief based on claims of breach of contract, fraud, and 
intentional misrepresentation, and looked to foreclose on the property. In October 2019, the 
parties settled. 
As part of this settlement agreement, Vintro provided Sinmier a deed in lieu of 
foreclosure to Maui Sands. The deed was “considered payment in full of Vintro’s monetary 
obligations under the Note or Mortgage.” R.119 -1 at 6. In addition, the agreement required 
Vintro and Inderjit Grewal —Vintro’s owner—to pay Sinmier $627,375 within nine months, 
secured by a consent judgment. The deed in lieu of foreclosure noted that Vintro and Grewal 
“will receive a release of liability on the note” as consideration for their conveyance of Maui 
Sands to Sinmier. R.76-1 at 2. 
 After executing the settlement agreement and accepting the deed in lieu of foreclosure, 
Sinmier filed this lawsuit against Bankers, Everest, and EverSports. 

No. 25-4018 Sinmier, LLC v. Everest Indemnity Ins. Co., et al. Page 4 

As to Bankers, Sinmier sought relief based on breach of contract as a third -party 
beneficiary, negligence, negligence per se, misrepresentation, and fraud. As to Everest, Sinmier 
sought relief as a third -party beneficiary based on breach of contract and liability for 
EverSports’s negligence as Everest’s agent. As to EverSports, Sinmier sought relief as a third -
party beneficiary based on breach of contract. 
 The district court granted summary judgment to each defendant and entered final 
judgment. 
II. 
We give fresh review to the district court’s summary judgment orders and draw all 
reasonable factual inferences in favor of the non -movant, Sinmier. See Peffer v. Stephens , 880 
F.3d 256, 260, 262 (6th Cir. 2018). All agree that Ohio law governs the case, meaning that we 
must “predict what the Ohio Supreme Court would do if confronted with” this question. Himmel 
v. Ford Motor Co. , 342 F.3d 593, 598 (6th Cir. 2003). In the absence of an on -point Ohio 
Supreme Court decision, we may look to decisions of the Ohio intermediate courts. Lukas v. 
McPeak, 730 F.3d 635, 638 (6th Cir. 2013). 
The key issue on appeal is whether the settlement agreement extinguished Sinmier’s 
insurable mortgagee interest. If the agreement ended that interest, Sinmier has no basis for relief 
because it brought each of these claims in its capacity as a mortgagee. And Sinmier has forfeited 
any argument that its negligence claims exist independently of its mortgagee interest. 
A mortgagee’s insurable interest exists to protect payment of the debt and dissipates 
when the borrower pays the debt or the lender releases it. A mortgage gives rise to an insurable 
interest in a mortgagee—here, Sinmier. See N. Assurance Co. v. Nat’l Guarantee & Fin. Co. , 21 
Ohio Law Abs. 641, 643 (Ct. App. 1936). This interest extends, however, only “to the amount of 
[the] debt.” McDonald v. Black’s Adm’r , 20 Ohio 185, 194 (1851). A mortgage does not etch 
into stone the mortgagee’s insurable interest. When the underlying debt decreases, the 
mortgagee’s insurable interest reduces in tandem. And when the debt ends, the mortgagee’s 
insurable interest ends. Barwick v. State Farm Fire & Cas. Ins. Co. , No. 24526, 2011 -Ohio-
No. 25-4018 Sinmier, LLC v. Everest Indemnity Ins. Co., et al. Page 5 

5689, ¶¶ 35–36 (Ct. App. Nov. 4, 2011); see also Lee v. Royal Indem. Co. , 108 F.3d 651, 656 
(6th Cir. 1997). 
In Barwick, a bank holding a mortgage purchased the underlying home at a sheriff’s sale 
after a fire loss. 2011-Ohio-5689 ¶ 36. The Ohio Court of Appeals held that the amount the 
bank received in the sale partially extinguished its interest in any insurance proceeds. Id. In 
reaching this conclusion, the court leaned on a Tennessee Supreme Court decision to the same 
effect. See id. ¶¶ 34–36 (discussing Benton Banking Co. v. Tenn. Farmers Mut. Ins. Co. , 906 
S.W.2d 436, 439 (Tenn. 1995)). While “[t]he mortgagee’s interest in the insurance proceeds is 
recognized as security for the payment of the debt,” Benton Banking explained, that reality lasts 
only as long as the debt does. 906 S.W.2d at 439. “[O]nce the debt is paid by some other means, 
any right to the insurance is thereby extinguished.” Id. 
This is not a new idea. What Ohio and Tennessee do in this area matches what other 
States do and indeed turns on a foundational principle of insurance law. See, e.g., Nationwide 
Mut. Fire Ins. Co. v. Wilborn , 279 So.2d 460, 463 (Ala. 1973); Fireman’s Fund Mortg. Corp. v. 
Allstate Ins. Co., 838 P.2d 790, 795 (Alaska 1992) (noting that “most courts have held that a 
subsequent foreclosure by a mortgagee either partially or completely divests the mortgagee of its 
rights under the insurance contract”); Burritt Mut. Sav. Bank of New Britain v. Transamerica Ins. 
Co., 428 A.2d 333, 338 (Conn. 1980); Power Bldg. & Loan Ass’n v. Ajax Fire Ins. Co. , 164 A. 
410, 411 (N.J. 1933) (“[A]fter the foreclosure sale and the satisfaction of the plaintiff’s debt, it 
ceased to have any interest as mortgagee in the premises covered by the policy.”); 5A J. 
Appleman, Insurance Law and Practice § 3403, at 302 (1970) (“[T]he full or partial 
extinguishment of the mortgage debt itself, whether prior to or subsequent to the loss, will 
preclude, to the extent thereof, any recovery on the policy by the mortgagee.”); 5 Couch on 
Insurance 2d §§ 29:75–77 (1960). 
Gauged by this well -established standard, Sinmier extinguished its insurable interest in 
the property when it signed the settlement agreement and accepted a deed to Maui Sands in lieu 
of foreclosure. Vintro, Grewal, and Sinmier agreed that the conveyance “shall be considered 
payment in full of Vintro’s monetary obligations under the Note or Mortgage.” R.119-1 at 6. To 
the same end, the parties agreed that, “[u]pon receipt of the Deed in Lieu of Foreclosure, Sinmier 
No. 25-4018 Sinmier, LLC v. Everest Indemnity Ins. Co., et al. Page 6 

shall fully release Vintro from any liability or responsibility it may have to pay any deficiency 
amount following the sale of Maui Sands, whether by foreclosure sale or otherwise.” R.119 -1 at 
5. In freely and voluntarily ending Vintro’s mortgage debt to it, Sinmier likewise ended its 
insurable interest as a mortgagee. 
That means Sinmier’s claims against Bankers, Everest, and EverSports fail as a matter of 
law. Each claim rises or falls with the existence or absence of a mortgagee interest. Sinmier did 
not possess any other interest in Maui Sands. It was not an owner. It was not an investor. It was 
a “mere creditor, who ha[d] a specific lien on the property for the payment of [its] debts.” Rands 
v. Kendall, 15 Ohio 671, 680 (1846). Release of the mortgage debt “destroy[ed]” its mortgagee 
interest “as to all the world.” Id. Sinmier’s claims all turn on the same proposition: The 
defendants wronged it when they issued insurance policies that came and went without 
protecting its mortgagee interest. In the absence of such an interest, its claims against the 
defendants are not cognizable ones. 
Trying to fend off this conclusion, Sinmier argues that the settlement agreement and the 
deed arrangement created ambiguous, conflicting terms. While the settlement agreement 
purported to fully release Vintro’s mortgage debt obligation, the deed provided that “the 
Mortgage shall

leads.caseName: NORHAVEN PARTNERS, LLC v. BARTOW COUNTY
leads.text:
SECOND DIVISION
 DOYLE, P. J.,
 DAVIS and WHITAKER, JJ.

 NOTICE: Motions for reconsideration must be
 received no later than 4:30 pm on the 10th day after
 the decision was issued to be deemed timely filed.
 https://www.gaappeals.gov/rules

 November 2, 2026

In the Court of Appeals of Georgia
 A26A1626. NORHAVEN PARTNERS, LLC et al. v. BARTOW
 COUNTY et al.

 DOYLE, Presiding Judge.

 Norhaven Partners, LLC, and Peeples Owner LLC (collectively, “Norhaven”)

filed a petition for review of the Bartow County Commissioner’s grant of a conditional

use permit (“CUP”) to Justin Rice and Rice Commercial Investments, Inc.,

(collectively, “Rice”) to build a waste processing facility next to a proposed

residential development. The trial court initially disposed of several arguments raised

in the petition but remanded for the commissioner to make further findings of fact and

conclusions of law as to the remaining arguments. On remand, the commissioner

made factual findings and legal conclusions as directed, and after a hearing, the trial

court rejected Norhaven’s remaining arguments. Norhaven appealed, arguing that the
 trial court erred by (1) reviewing only the written transcript of the public hearing

before the commissioner; (2) remanding the case to the commissioner to make factual

findings where the record was amenable to only one interpretation; and (3) denying

the petition after the commissioner ignored the trial court’s instructions on remand.

For the reasons that follow, we affirm.

 Our review of a quasi-judicial decision of an agency of a local government by

way of a petition for review

 requires us to determine that the findings of fact are supported by any
 evidence and to examine the soundness of the conclusions of law that are
 based upon the findings of fact. ... [W]hen we review a superior court’s
 order in a[ quasi-judicial] proceeding, our duty is not to review whether
 the record supports the superior court’s decision but whether the record
 supports the final decision of the [quasi-judicial] agency. ... [W]e review
 legal conclusions de novo.

Beacon Media, LLC v. City of Atlanta, 379 Ga. App. 477, 478 (929 SE2d 40) (2026)

(cleaned up).

 So viewed, the record reflects that in January 2023, Bartow County approved

conceptual site plans submitted by Norhaven to develop a 97-unit townhome

community on residentially zoned property. By October 2023, the development plans

for this townhome community, known as the Overlook on Pettit, had been fully

 2
 approved by the county, which approved Norhaven’s application for a land use

disturbance permit for the development.

 Adjacent to, and east of, the site of Norhaven’s planned residential

development is property zoned heavy industrial owned by Rice. Rice had been using

the property for a mulch materials processing, wood shredding, and rock crushing

operation prior to its July 2, 2024 application for a CUP to expand the use of the

property to include a recovered materials processing and solid waste handling facility

for construction and demolition materials. At the time of Rice’s CUP application, no

construction had begun on Norhaven’s residential development, but based on an

overlay of Rice’s proposed site plan and Norhaven’s development plans, 46 of the 97

proposed townhomes would be within 1,000 feet of the proposed waste handling area.

 Relevant to this appeal, Section 9.5.6 of the Bartow County Zoning Ordinance

provides that “[n]o waste handling area (as measured from the chain link fence

boundary) may be located within one thousand (1,000) feet of any residential dwelling

(so used at the time of the application).” Section 3.1 of the zoning ordinance provides

that “[t]he word ‘used’ or ‘occupied’ as applied to any land or building shall be

construed to include the words ‘intended, arranged[,] or designed to be used or

occupied.’” Section 3.2 of the ordinance defines “dwelling” as “[a] building or other

 3
 structure designed, arranged, or used for temporary or permanent living quarters for

one or more persons.” This Section further defines “structure” as “[a]nything

constructed or erected, the use of which requires location on the ground, or

attachment to something having location on the ground.”

 In August 2024, a public hearing on Rice’s CUP application was held before the

Bartow County Planning Commission, which voted to recommend approval of the

CUP with certain conditions, such as construction of a berm along the boundary of the

property bordering residential properties and a prohibition on the incineration of

waste. Rice’s CUP application then came before the Bartow County Commissioner

for a public hearing on September 4, 2024. Representatives of Norhaven, as well as

members of the public, appeared at the hearing and voiced their opposition to the

CUP. In particular, representatives of Norhaven argued that based on Rice’s proposed

site plan, approval of the CUP would result in a violation of Section 9.5.6 of the

Bartow County Zoning Ordinance because Rice’s waste processing facility would be

within 1,000 feet of 46 of the townhomes planned for construction as part of

Norhaven’s residential development. At the conclusion of the hearing, the

commissioner approved Rice’s CUP application, subject to the conditions

recommended by the planning commission, as well as the additional condition per the

 4
 zoning ordinance that a “1,000-foot separation distance from residential homes from

the proposed solid waste handling facilities shall be in place and shall be maintained.”

 On October 3, 2024, Norhaven filed a petition for review of the commissioner’s

approval of the CUP, naming Rice and Bartow County as a respondents. Relevant to

this appeal, the petition alleged that the approval of Rice’s CUP application violated

Section 9.5.6 of the Bartow County Zoning Ordinance in that the proposed waste

processing facility would be within 1,000 feet of residential dwellings and that the

approval was therefore void. The trial court convened a hearing on the petition on July

9, 2025. At the hearing, counsel for Norhaven argued that a dwelling need not be

constructed in order to trigger application of Section 9.5.6 of the zoning ordinance;

it merely had to be “intended, arranged, or designed to be used” pursuant to Section

3.1 of the ordinance. Counsel for Rice countered that Section 9.5.6 of the ordinance

required a 1,000-foot separation distance only as measured from residential dwellings

constructed at the time the CUP application was submitted, citing Section 3.2 of the

ordinance, which defines “dwelling” as a “building or other structure designed,

arranged, or used for temporary or permanent living quarters for one or more

persons.”

 On September 3, 2025, the trial court entered an order on Norhaven’s petition

 5
 for review. Relevant to this appeal, the trial court interpreted OCGA § 5-3-5(a)(1) to

confine the scope of its review to the transcript of the hearing before the

commissioner, to the exclusion of any issue not specifically raised at this hearing. The

trial court also remanded the case to the commissioner for determination of “whether

any portion of a waste handling area, as measured from the chain link fence boundary,

is located within one thousand (1,000) feet of any residential dwelling (intended,

arranged, or designed to be used).”

 On remand, the commissioner made a written finding of fact that Rice’s

proposed “waste handling area, as measured from the chain link fence boundary, was

located at least 1,000 feet from any residential dwelling being used at the time of the

[a]pplication.” In support of this finding, the commissioner cited testimony from the

September 4, 2024 hearing that Norhaven had completed some site work but had not

yet started construction of any townhomes pursuant to its residential development

plan.

 Following entry of the commissioner’s written findings, the case was

transmitted back to the trial court, which convened a second hearing on Norhavan’s

petition for review on December 17, 2025. There, counsel for Norhaven challenged

the commissioner’s finding that Rice’s proposed waste handling facility would be at

 6
 least 1,000 feet from any residential dwelling on the grounds (1) that it was not

supported by any evidence, and (2) that it ignored the trial court’s remand

instructions by failing to consider Section 9.5.6 of the zoning ordinance in conjunction

with Section 3.1 of the ordinance, under which Norhaven’s proposed residential

building sites should be considered buildings that were “intended, arranged, or

designed to be used” as residential dwellings.

 On January 5, 2026, the trial court entered a final order denying the petition and

affirming the commissioner’s approval of Rice’s CUP application. In its order, the

trial court ruled that the commissioner had complied with the trial court’s instructions

on remand to make written findings of fact. Additionally, the trial court ruled that the

commissioner was required to consider Section 3.1 of the zoning ordinance and “any

other applicable code when determining whether a waste handling facility is within

1,000 feet of a residential dwelling.” Although the trial court’s order does not

explicitly deny Norhaven’s argument that the approval of Rice’s CUP application was

void for violating Sections 9.5.6 and 3.1 of the zoning ordinance, subsequent

correspondence among the trial court and parties clarifies that it was the trial court’s

intention to do so. Norhaven filed an application for discretionary appeal, which this

Court granted, and this appeal followed.

 7
  1. Norhaven contends that the trial court erred by construing OCGA § 5-3-

5(a)(1) to confine the scope of its review to the written transcript of the public hearing

before the commissioner. This contention is without merit.

 OCGA § 5-3-5(a)(1) provides that in reviewing the decision of a lower

judicatory, “a reviewing court shall ... [r]eview only matters raised in the record of the

proceedings in the lower judicatory.” When interpreting statutory language, Georgia

courts are to “presume that the General Assembly meant what it said and said what

it meant.” Deal v. Coleman, 294 Ga. 170, 172(1)(a) (751 SE2d 337) (2013) (quotation

marks omitted). In so doing, we “must afford the statutory text its plain and ordinary

meaning, ... view the statutory text in the context in which it appear, and ... read the

statutory text in its most natural and reasonable way.” Chestnut Ridge, LLC v. Hall

County Bd. of Tax Assessors, 323 Ga. 150, 155(1) (924 SE2d 331) (2025) (quotation

marks omitted). “[I]f the statutory text is clear and unambiguous, we attribute to the

statute its plaining meaning, and our search for statutory meaning is at and end.” Id.

(quotation marks omitted).

 Here, the phrase “matters raised in the record of the proceeding in the lower

judicatory” plainly refers to all materials submitted to or considered by the lower

judicatory during the course of the relevant proceeding. To the extent that the trial

 8
 court interpreted OCGA § 5-3-5(a)(1) to confine the scope of its review to the

transcript of the hearing before the commissioner, to the exclusion of issues not

specifically raised at this hearing, such as Section 3.1 or other applicable provisions of

the zoning ordinance, Rice’s CUP application, or other materials submitted to or

considered by the commissioner but not directly addressed at the hearing, the trial

court erred.

 But a successful enumeration of error requires a showing of both error and

harm. See Alligood v. Piedmont Med. Care Corp., Inc., 369 Ga. App. 171, 172(1) (892

SE2d 790) (2023) (“An appellant must show harm as well as error to prevail on

appeal; error to be reversible must be harmful.”) (quotation marks omitted). Here,

although the trial court purported to limit its review to the transcript of the hearing

before the c

Filed 10/30/26 Four Dimensions, Inc. v. Wang CA6 
NOT TO BE PUBLISHED IN OFFICIAL REPORTS 

California Rules of Court, rule 8.1115(a), prohibits courts and parties from citing or relying on opinions not certified for 
publication or ordered published, except as specified by rule 8.1115(b). This opinion has not been certified for publication 
or ordered published for purposes of rule 8.1115. 

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 

SIXTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 

FOUR DIMENSIONS, INC., 

 Plaintiff and Respondent, 

 v. 

LOUIS WANG et al., 

 Defendants and Appellants. 

 H053331 
 (Santa Clara County 
 Super. Ct. No. 24CV449015) 

This appeal is from the denial of a special motion to strike under Code of Civil 
Procedure section 425.16, the anti-SLAPP statute. (Subsequent undesignated statutory 
references are to the Code of Civil Procedure.) 
Plaintiff Four Dimensions, Inc. (Four Dimensions) is a semiconductor technology 
company based in the Bay Area. After its founder died, Four Dimensions’ board of 
directors decided to explore a sale, and defendants Louis Wang and Sherry Li attempted 
to acquire the company. Negotiations between Four Dimensions and defendants fell 
through, and Four Dimensions instead entered into negotiations with a Chinese company, 
Wuxi Zhuohai Technology Co. Ltd. (WZH). However, after Wang warned WZH about 
the regulatory obstacles it would face as a foreign entity trying to acquire a United States 
semiconductor company, WZH declined to pursue the acquisition. 
Four Dimensions sued Wang and Li for tortious interference and other torts, and 
defendants in turn filed a motion to strike under the anti-SLAPP statute, arguing that 
 2 
Wang’s warnings to WZH and then to Four Dimensions and its shareholders were 
protected activities under the statute because they concerned matters of public interest: 
namely, national security risks and regulatory restrictions imposed on foreign entities 
acquiring domestic semiconductor companies. The trial court denied the motion, 
reasoning that defendants failed to demonstrate that Four Dimensions’ claims arose out of 
protected activity under the anti-SLAPP statute. Defendants appeal this ruling. 
As explained below, we affirm. National security and the regulation of foreign 
acquisition of U.S. semiconductor technology are issues of public interest. However, 
Wang’s warnings do not fall within the anti-SLAPP statute’s definition of protected 
activity. Because the warnings evidenced in the record were cursory, and they were 
privately made for private purposes and remained private, the warnings are not covered 
by the anti-SLAPP statute’s catchall provision (§ 425.16, subd. (e)(4)), which applies 
only to speech and other conduct that contributes to the public discourse on issues of 
public interest. (See, e.g., FilmOn.com Inc. v. DoubleVerify Inc. (2019) 7 Cal.5th 133, 
149-152 (FilmOn).) The pending official proceedings provision (§ 425.16, subd. (e)(2)) 
is also inapplicable because WZH decided not to acquire Four Dimensions (due to 
Wang’s warnings), and there were no official proceedings pending concerning the 
acquisition. 
Defendants’ motion to strike was properly denied, and the order denying the 
motion is affirmed. 
I. BACKGROUND 
In reviewing an order denying a motion to strike under the anti-SLAPP statute, we 
consider “ ‘the pleadings, and supporting and opposing affidavits … [stating the facts] 
upon which the liability or defense is based’ (§ 425.16, subd. (b)(2)),” accepting as true 
evidence presented by the opposing party. (Soukup v. Law Offices of Herbert Hafif 
(2006) 39 Cal.4th 260, 269, fn. 3.) 
 3 
A. Four Dimensions 
Four Dimensions produces semiconductor probing systems used to test the 
conductivity of electronic components in computers and other electronic systems and 
devices. Four Dimensions’ customers include semiconductor manufacturers, defense 
contractors, and government agencies, including the former Department of Defense. 
Four Dimensions was founded in 1978 by James T.C. Chen. Mr. Chen passed 
away in February 2021, and in 2023 the company’s board of directors authorized its 
management to explore a sale. 
B. Louis Wang and Sherry Li 
Louis Wang is a tech investor. In 2023, he was a partner in and director of a 
Singapore-based middle market, specialty private equity firm, Asia-IO Partners 
International Pte., Ltd. (Asia-IO). In June 2023, Four Dimensions and Asia-IO executed 
a nondisclosure agreement, which Wang signed on Asia-IO’s behalf. In the agreement, 
Asia-IO promised to use confidential information obtained from Four Dimensions solely 
in evaluating, negotiating, and consummating a potential business transaction with the 
company. 
Under the nondisclosure agreement, Wang received confidential information from 
Four Dimensions, and in October 2023 Asia-IO and Four Dimensions entered into a 
non-binding letter of intent in which Four Dimensions agreed to deal exclusively with 
Asia-IO. However, in December 2023 Wang informed Four Dimensions that Asia-IO had 
decided to withdraw from the proposed acquisition. According to Wang, Asia-IO was 
concerned that Four Dimensions had not obtained a formal export classification from the 
Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and an attempted acquisition 
of Four Dimensions by a foreign entity would be reviewed, and possibly blocked, by the 
Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), a federal executive 
branch committee chaired by the Secretary of the Treasury. (See 50 U.S.C. § 4565.) 
 4 
However, Wang informed Four Dimensions that his wife Sherry Li and her 
American-registered limited liability company, Omni Ventures Partners, LLC (Omni), 
were interested in acquiring Four Dimensions. For several months, Omni conducted due 
diligence on Four Dimensions, and in February 2024 it made a proposal for acquiring the 
company. However, in March 2024, after Wang contacted Four Dimensions’ 
employee-shareholders about the potential transaction without the company’s 
authorization, Four Dimensions terminated negotiations with Omni. 
Nevertheless, in May 2024, Wang submitted a new term sheet for an Omni 
acquisition. However, Four Dimensions informed Wang that it was talking with other 
potential buyers. 
C. WZH 
In June 2024, Four Dimensions entered into discussions with WZH, a Chinese 
company allegedly with financial backing from Chinese state-controlled investors tied to 
Chinese semiconductor and military-industrial policies. 
In July 2024, WZH sent Four Dimensions a draft letter of intent proposing terms 
for acquiring Four Dimensions. Four Dimensions responded with comments, and in 
mid-July the parties agreed that Four Dimensions’ counsel would draft a more formal 
terms sheet. 
However, that same month, Wang spoke with WZH representatives. According to 
Wang, these discussions “were strictly limited to publicly available information 
concerning general CFIUS scrutiny and regulatory compliance matters, without any 
explicit mention of 4D [Four Dimensions],” though he admitted commenting on “WZH’s 
regulatory risks associated with a potential acquisition of a U.S. semiconductor 
company.” 
The following month WZH withdrew from the proposed acquisition of Four 
Dimensions. One of the reasons that WZH gave for doing so was that it had been 
 5 
contacted by Wang who “made numerous comments about why [WZH] should not do the 
transaction and shared … Four Dimensions’ Confidential Information.” 
D. The Proceedings Below 
In October 2024, Four Dimensions sued Wang and Li as well as Asia-IO. Four 
Dimensions asserted five claims: breach of the nondisclosure agreement Wang signed for 
Asia-IO, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, intentional 
interference, negligent interference, and aiding and abetting a breach of fiduciary duty. 
Specifically, Four Dimensions alleged that Wang and Asia-IO breached the nondisclosure 
agreement and the covenant of good faith in that agreement by disclosing confidential 
information to WZH and to Li and Omni, as well as failing to return or destroy such 
information. Four Dimensions also alleged that Wang and Li both intentionally and 
negligently interfered with WZH’s potential acquisition of Four Dimensions by 
improperly sharing confidential information and by disparaging Four Dimensions’ 
business and management. Finally, Four Dimensions alleged that Wang and Li aided and 
abetted a breach of fiduciary duty by a Four Dimensions employee in revealing the 
potential transaction with WZH. 
Wang and Li (but not Asia-IO) filed a motion to strike under the anti-SLAPP 
statute. In support of the motion, defendants submitted a declaration from Wang, who, 
among other things, averred that in July 2024 he participated in a call with WZH 
representatives in which he discussed “general CFIUS scrutiny and regulatory 
compliance matters” and “WZH’s regulatory risks associated with a potential acquisition 
of a U.S. semiconductor company.” Based on this declaration, defendants asserted that 
Four Dimensions’ complaint targeted speech concerning matters of public interest: 
“national security risks and regulatory compliance issues arising from a proposed sale of 
4D [Four Dimensions]” to WZH. Defendants argued that this speech was a protected 
activity under the anti-SLAPP statute because it was covered by the statute’s catchall 
provision for “speech on matters of public interest” and by the pending official 
 6 
proceedings provision for matters “under active consideration by government regulatory 
bodies.” Defendants did not identify specific allegations or claims protected by the 
anti-SLAPP statute, nor did they explain how any of Four Dimensions’ claims arise out of 
protected activity. 
The trial court denied the motion to strike. The court ruled that defendants had 
failed to satisfy their threshold burden of showing that Four Dimensions’ claims arise out 
of protected activity because defendants did not demonstrate that they engaged in 
protected activity under the anti-SLAPP statute. The court ruled the catchall provision 
inapplicable because defendants failed to show which, if any, of Four Dimensions’ claims 
arise out of Wang’s warnings to WZH or to establish that those warnings contributed to 
public debate over those issues. The trial court also ruled the pending official 
proceedings provision inapplicable because defendants failed to show that Wang’s 
warnings concerned an issue under consideration in an official proceeding. 
Wang and Li filed timely notices of appeal from the denial of their anti-SLAPP 
motion. (See § 425.16, subd. (i) [authorizing interlocutory appeals from the denial of 
anti-SLAPP motions].) 
II. DISCUSSION 
On appeal, defendants Wang and Li argue that Four Dimensions’ claims against 
them arise out of the warnings that Wang gave to WZH and that these warnings are 
protected activity under the anti-SLAPP statute’s catchall and pending official 
proceedings provisions. We review de novo the trial court’s rulings on these issues. 
(See, e.g., Park v. Board of Trustees of California State University (2017) 2 Cal.5th 1057, 
1067 (Park).) However, before doing so, we briefly review the anti-SLAPP statute. 
A. The Anti-SLAPP Statute 
“The anti-SLAPP law was enacted ‘to protect nonprofit corporations and common 
citizens “from large corporate entities and trade associations” in petitioning 
government.’ ” (FilmOn, supra, 7 Cal.5th at p. 143.) This statute combats “strategic 
 7 
lawsuits against public participation (SLAPPs): ‘lawsuits brought primarily to chill the 
valid exercise of the constitutional rights of freedom of speech and petition for the redress 
of grievances.’ ” (Geiser v. Kuhns (2022) 13 Cal.5th 1238, 1242 (Geiser), quoting 
§ 425.16, subd. (a).) “In the paradigmatic SLAPP suit, a well-funded developer limits 
free expression by imposing litigation costs on citizens who protest, write letters, and

 PENNSYLVANIA

In the Court of Common Pleas of Philadelphia County

BEFORE: OLSON, J., DUBOW, J., and FORD ELLIOTT, P.J.E. 
MEMORANDUM BY FORD ELLIOTT, P.J.E.: FILED NOVEMBER 2, 2026 
 Sallah Abdulla appeals pro se from the judgment entered following a 
non-jury trial during which the court found in favor of the defendant-appellees, 
Selina Inc., Budo Bunul, and Elebeh Mohamed,1 in the amount of $0.00. 
Abdulla argues reversal is required on grounds: (1) of judicial bias; (2) that 
the court erred in not recognizing the existence of a verbal lease between 
himself and Bunul; (3) that Abdulla proved he was illegally evicted by the 
defendant-appellees; and (4) that the coordinate jurisdiction rule is 
inapplicable to this case. We affirm. 
 The trial court summarized the factual and procedural history of this 
____________________________________________ 
 Retired Senior Judge assigned to the Superior Court. 

1 “Mohamed” is alternatively spelled “Mohammed” elsewhere in the record. 
See, e.g., Trial Court Opinion, 1/12/26, at 1. 

J-A19042-26 
- 2 - 
matter, in relevant part, as follows: 

The core disagreement in this matter concerns the legality of 
Abdulla’s eviction from an Airbnb rental establishment and alleged 
past due rent. 

On October 21, 2021, Abdulla initiated a civil action in equity in 
the First Judicial District of Pennsylvania Civil Division by filing a 
pro se complaint against Bunul, Selina Inc., and Elebeh, which was 
docketed under October Term 2022 No. 01723. Abdulla’s 
complaint asserted that on October 8, 2021, the defendant-
appellees had engaged in an illegal self-help eviction and 
unlawfully evicted Abdulla from a “rental” unit at 1528 N. Mascher 
St., Philadelphia, PA. Commensurate with his filing of the 
complaint, Abdulla filed an [“]emergency petition to reverse illegal 
eviction[”] seeking to restore his access and possession to the 
subject property. 

[Judge] Paula Patrick[2] . . . entered a rule and order scheduling a 
virtual hearing for October 28, 2021, and requiring Abdulla to 
effectuate personal service of the complaint and emergency 
motion and rule upon all defendant-appellees and to provide 
advance proof of service by October 25, 2021. Docket records 
reflected Abdulla’s unsuccessful and untimely service and proof of 
filing of that service. 

Upon reassignment, on October 26, 2021, [Judge] Joshua Roberts 
. . . entered a rule and order scheduling a virtual hearing for 
October 28, 2021[,] and requiring Abdulla to effectuate personal 
service of the complaint and emergency motion and rule upon all 
defendant-appellees and to provide advance proof of service by 
October 25, 2021. 

On November 1, 2021, and as modified on November 9, 202[1], 
[Judge] Roberts entered emergency injunctive orders granting 
Abdulla temporary restoration of access and possession of the 
subject property. Judge Roberts scheduled [a] further hearing 
upon Abdulla’s filing of a motion for contempt. 
____________________________________________ 
2 All judges referenced herein are judges on the Court of Common Pleas of 
Philadelphia County. 

J-A19042-26 
- 3 - 

Thereafter, Steven Lynas, Esquire[,] entered [an appearance] as 
counsel on behalf of Selina Inc. and Elebeh in the civil action and 
filed preliminary objections to the complaint and a motion for 
reconsideration of Judge Roberts’ order dated November 1, 2021. 
Rachelle Waitz, Esquire[,] entered her appearance on behalf of 
Bunul, and filed a commensurate motion[] for reconsideration of 
[] Judge Roberts’ order and preliminary objections to the 
complaint. Additional responsive pleadings were filed by Abdulla. 
The respective motions for reconsideration were rescheduled for 
hearing on December 6, 2021. Thereafter, Judge Roberts vacated 
his respective orders of November 1, 2021[,] and November 9, 
2021[,] and denied Abdulla’s previously requested forms of 
injunctive relief[, in effect expressly dissolving the then-existing 
preliminary injunction]. 

On January 4, 2022, in due course of the underlying civil action, 
[Judge] Jaqueline Allen sustained the preliminary objections of 
Selina Inc. and Elebeh to the complaint and directed Abdulla to 
timely file more specific pleadings. On January 18, 2022, [Judge] 
Charles Cunningham denied Abdulla’s motion for judgment on the 
pleadings. Abdulla filed an amended complaint on January 31, 
202[2]. 

Following [a] settlement conference and case management 
conference, a corresponding scheduling order was entered. On 
February 14, 2022[, Judge] Ann Butchart sustained Bunul’s . . . 
preliminary objections to Abdulla’s complaint and directed Abdulla 
to file an amended complaint with more specific pleading[s] within 
twenty (20) days. 

On February 23, 2022, . . . Elebeh and Selina Inc. filed an answer 
with new matter to Abdulla’s complaint. Thereafter[,] Judge 
Butchart entered an order deeming Bunul’s preliminary objections 
to Abdulla’s complaint to be moot. 

Additional preliminary objections to Abdulla’s amended complaint 
were filed . . . [by] Bunul on March 7, 2022. Abdulla filed an 
answer. On April 25, 2022, [Judge] Mich[a]el Erdos entered an 
order overruling Bunul’s . . . preliminary objections on April 25, 
2022. [Bunul then filed his] answer with new matter to Abdulla’s 
amended complaint on May 4, 2022. 

On May 13, 2022, Abdulla filed a miscellaneous motion to strike 
J-A19042-26 
- 4 - 
the jury demand and on May 31, 2022, he filed preliminary 
objections. Because the motion to strike the jury demand 
appeared to be unopposed, [Judge] Denis Cohen granted the 
motion to strike and transferred the matter to non-jury trial 
expedited programs on June 7, 2022. 

On June 16, 2022, [Bunul filed an amended answer to the new 
matter,] which rendered Abdulla’s preliminary objections moot. 
Abdulla filed additional . . . preliminary objections . . . on July 5, 
2022. Also, in July 2022[,] the underlying matter was listed for 
pre-trial conference and placed in the trial ready pool. 

. . . [After proceedings that are irrelevant to the present appeal, 
which necessitated placing the case into deferred status, the case 
ultimately proceeded to a non-jury trial on April 7, 2025]. 
Following oral argument, [the trial c]ourt[, Judge Anne Marie 
Coyle,] found in favor of defendant-appellees. On that same date, 
Abdulla filed a motion to reconsider Judge Roberts[’] December 7, 
2021 order. On April 9, 2025, Abdulla filed a [“]motion to 
recuse[”] seeking [the trial c]ourt to vacate its April 7 findings and 
recuse itself from a future trial in this matter. Judge Robe[r]ts 
denied the motion and on April 15th, Abdulla filed a post[-]trial 
motion seeking [the trial c]ourt [to] vacate its April 7th order and 
to relist the matter before Judge Roberts. On April 16, Abdulla’s 
motion to disqualify [the trial c]ourt was denied. On April 24, a 
notice of appeal . . . was filed to the Superior Court of 
Pennsylvania. [Thereafter, Abdulla filed] a 7-page [Pennsylvania 
Rule of Appellate Procedure] 1925(b) statement [cumulatively 
raising ten issues]. 
Trial Court Opinion, 1/12/26, at 1-12 (party names altered; unnecessary 
capitalization omitted). 
 Preliminarily, we note that Abdulla’s brief violates our appellate rules in 
multiple ways. See generally Pa.R.A.P. 2111(a) (designating the necessary 
components of an appellate brief); see also Pa.R.A.P. 2117(b) (prohibiting 
the inclusion of argument within the statement of the case). Most importantly, 
however, although his “Questions Preserved” portion of his brief contains 
twelve “questions,” see Appellant’s Brief at 7-8, the argument section of his 
J-A19042-26 
- 5 - 
brief only contains four headings. See id. at 14-20. 
Rule 2119(a) establishes that “[t]he argument shall be divided into as 
many parts as there are questions to be argued; and shall have at the head 
of each part--in distinctive type or in type distinctively displayed--the 
particular point treated therein, followed by such discussion and citation of 
authorities as are deemed pertinent.” Pa.R.A.P. 2119(a). Although we 
recognize Abdulla’s status as a pro se litigant and are willing to liberally 
construe the materials he has filed, we also stress that, “pro se status confers 
no special benefit upon the appellant.” S.S. v. T.J., 212 A.3d 1026, 1032 (Pa. 
Super. 2019) (citation omitted). And, as a further point of emphasis, we 
caution that “any person choosing to represent himself in a legal proceeding 
must, to a reasonable extent, assume that his lack of expertise and legal 
training will be his undoing.” Id. (citation omitted). 
With all of that in mind, given the incongruency between his questions 
presented and the number of arguments contained in his argument section, 
we endeavor to interpret his claims as much as is practicable. Our disposition 
will be guided by Abdulla’s argument headings, which will be addressed in 
seriatim. 
As this case involves the appeal of a judgment entered following a non-
jury trial, our standard of review is as follows: 

Our appellate role in cases arising from non-jury trial verdicts is 
to determine whether the findings of the trial court are supported 
by competent evidence and whether the trial court committed 
error in any application of the law. The findings of fact of the trial 
judge must be given the same weight and effect on appeal as the 
J-A19042-26 
- 6 - 
verdict of a jury. We consider the evidence in a light most 
favorable to the verdict winner. We will reverse the trial court only 
if its findings of fact are not supported by competent evidence in 
the record or if its findings are premised on an error of law. 
However, where the issue concerns a question of law, our scope 
of review is plenary. 
Bank of New York Mellon v. Bach, 159 A.3d 16, 19 (Pa. Super. 2017). 
First, Abdulla contends that Judge Coyle’s decision and judgment were 
motivated by bias, prejudice, and partiality. See Appellant’s Brief at 14. 
Abdulla asserts that she “declared her personal bias and prejudice towards 
the merits of the case in broad daylight.” Id. Although he highlights a specific 
portion of the trial transcript in which he alleges bias from the court, see id. 
quoting Non-Jury Trial, 4/7/25, at 7, review of the transcript confirms that he 
did not make a contemporaneous objection to the court’s statement he now 
challenges. Furthermore, Abdulla’s brief does not establish where and how he 
has preserved his averment of bias or, alternatively, when he sought recusal. 
See, e.g., Pa.R.A.P. 2119(e); see also Pa.R.A.P. 2117(c); Reily v. SEPTA, 
489 A.2d 1291, 1300 (Pa. 1985) (“Once the trial is completed with the entry 
of a verdict, a party[, who failed to make a timely, specific objection at trial 
as to recusal,] is deemed to have waived his right to have a judge disqualified, 
and if he has waived that issue, he cannot be heard to complain following an 
unfavorable result.”). Accordingly, Abdulla’s claim is unreviewable and 
warrants no relief. See Thorson v. EDDW, LLC, 309 A.3d 141, 148 (Pa. 
Super. 2024) (stating to preserve an issue for appeal, a litigant must make a 
timely, specific objection at trial); see also Pa.R.Civ.P. 227.1(b)(1), Note 
(“[I]f no objection is made, error which could have been corrected . . . during 
J-A19042-26 
- 7 - 
trial by timely objection may not constitute a ground for post-trial relief.”). 
In his second claim, Abdulla argues that there was a legitimate verbal 
lease establishing a landlord-tenant relationship between himself and Bunul, 
but that the court did not recognize its existence. Abdulla avers that he “had 
lived in the subject property for a ye

25-2539-cv 
Murray v. Newrez LLC & PHH Mortgage Corporation 

UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS 
FOR THE SECOND CIRCUIT 

August Term 2025 

(Argued: May 15, 2026 Decided: November 2, 2026) 

Docket No. 25-2539-cv 

SHERRY ANN MURRAY, 
Plaintiﬀ-Appellant, 

v. 

NEWREZ LLC, DBA SHELLPOINT MORTGAGE SERVICING, PHH MORTGAGE 
CORPORATION, DBA PHH MORTGAGE SERVICES, 
Defendants-Appellees. 

Before: NEWMAN, WESLEY, and PÉREZ, Circuit Judges. 
Appeal from a judgment of the District Court for the Eastern District of New 
York (Allyne R. Ross, District Judge) dismissing a second amended complaint 
brought pursuant to the Real Estate SeĴlement Procedures Act, 12 U.S.C. §§ 2601 
et seq ., seeking damages for increased interest and fees in connection with a 
2 

modiﬁed mortgage, legal fees for preparing a second qualiﬁed wriĴen request 
(“QWR”), and postage for mailing the second QWR. 
 Aﬃrmed. Judge Pérez dissents in part with a separate opinion. 

STEVEN AMSHEN, Petroﬀ Amshen LLP, 
Brooklyn, NY, for Plaintiﬀ-Appellant. 

ALI DEGAN (Schuyler B. Kraus, on the brief ), 
Hinshaw & Culbertson LLP, New York, NY, for 
Defendants-Appellees. 

 JON O. NEWMAN, Senior Circuit Judge: 
The Real Estate SeĴlement Procedures Act (“RESPA”), 12 U.S.C. §§ 2601 et 
seq., provides that “[i]f any servicer of a federally related mortgage loan receives a 
qualiﬁed wriĴen request [“QWR”] from the borrower . . . for information relating 
to the servicing of such loan , the servicer shall provide a wriĴen response 
acknowledging receipt of the correspondence within 5 days . . . unless the action 
requested is taken within such period.” Id. § 2605(e)(1)(A) (emphasis added). 
RESPA also provides that “[w]hoever fails to comply with any provision of 
this section shall be liable to the borrower for each such failure in the following 
amounts: . . . any actual damages to the borrower as a result of the failure,” id. 
3 

§ 2605(f)(1)(A), and “[i]n addition to the amounts under paragraph (1) . . . , in the 
case of any successful action under this section, the costs of the action, together with any 
aĴorney[’]s fees incurred in connection with such action as the court may determine to 
be reasonable under the circumstances.” Id. § 2605(f)(3) (emphases added). 
In this case, the plaintiﬀ Sherry Ann Murray sent a QWR to the defendants 
PHH Mortgage Corporation, the servicer of her loan, and Newrez LLC, the master 
servicer of her loan. Murray did not receive the required responses. The lawyer 
who prepared the ﬁrst QWR then prepared a second QWR to send to the 
defendants. Again she received no responses. 
In a second amended complaint, 1 the plaintiﬀ brought this RESPA action to 
recover “damages . . . resulting from the Defendants’ failure to acknowledge or 
respond to Plaintiﬀ’s multiple qualiﬁed wriĴen requests for information related to 
her mortgage account, which has prevented Plaintiﬀ from correcting errors to her 
account, including removing improper fees added to the loan balance . . . .” Second 
Amended Complaint ¶ 1. The improper fees and interest were alleged to be more 

1 The plaintiﬀ had ﬁled a ﬁrst amended complaint, alleging that the Defendants had “violated 
their duties to provide account information and to remedy servicing and account errors.” 
District Court Opinion 2. The District Court dismissed that complaint with leave to amend, 
because the plaintiﬀ “failed to allege damages.” Id. 
4 

than $70,277.15. Id. ¶¶ 16, 17, 94, 98. The plaintiﬀ also sought $225 for legal fees for 
preparing the second QWR and $3.20 for postage for mailing the second QWR. Id. 
¶ 98. 
The District Court (Allyne R. Ross, District Judge) denied all relief and 
dismissed the second amended complaint. Murray timely appealed. 
We ﬁrst consider the plaintiﬀ’s claim for allegedly improper interest and 
fees, claimed to be in excess of $70,277.15. This sum resulted from a modiﬁcation 
of the plaintiﬀ’s mortgage after the plaintiﬀ failed to make several monthly 
mortgage payments. Whether or not the plaintiﬀ is liable for the added interest 
and fees, they were added to her debt as a result of a mortgage modiﬁcation and 
had nothing to do with servicing the mortgage. They are therefore not recoverable 
in a RESPA action. 
We next consider whether RESPA requires the defendants to pay the 
plaintiﬀ the legal fee of $225, which she paid a lawyer to prepare the second QWR. 
We agree with the District Court that the lawyer’s fee was not “actual damages” 
within the meaning of RESPA. AĴorney’s fees are not actual damages under 
RESPA because the statute provides for such fees “[i]n addition to” actual damages. 
12 U.S.C. § 2605(f)(3); see WhiĴier v. Ocwen Loan Servicing, L.L.C., 594 Fed Appx. 
5 

833, 836-37 (5th Cir. 2014); Allen v. United Financial Mortgage Corp., 660 F. Supp. 2d 
1089, 1097 (N.D. Cal. 2009).2 
These courts can be considered to have made not only a textual argument 
but also to have applied, in eﬀect, the general principle of law that a speciﬁc section 
governs over a general section elsewhere in a statute. See, e.g., RadLAX Gateway 
Hotel, LLC v. Amalgamated Bank, 566 U.S. 639, 645 (2012) (“[I]t is a commonplace of 
statutory construction that the speciﬁc governs the general.”) (internal quotation 
marks omiĴed); Fourco Glass Co. v. Transmirra Products Corp., 353 U.S. 222, 228 
(1957) (“However inclusive may be the general language of a statute, it will not be 
held to apply to a maĴer speciﬁcally dealt with in another part of the same 
enactment.”) (internal quotation marks omiĴed); Davis v. Shah , 821 F.3d 231, 251 
(2d Cir. 2016) (“[A] speciﬁc provision takes precedence over a more general one.”) 
(internal quotation marks omiĴed). That principle is particularly applicable to this 
case where the speciﬁc provision explicitly mentions “aĴorney[’]s fees,” and the 
general provision uses the broad phrase “actual damages.” 

2 Our dissenting colleague cites Key Tronic Corp. v. United States , 511 U.S. 809 (1994), dissenting 
opinion 5, where the Supreme Court, in an environmental cleanup action, allowed the plaintiﬀ 
recovery of some aĴorney’s fees not incurred to pursue the litigation. However, the statutes at 
issue in that case, unlike RESPA, did not provide that recoverable “actual damages,” which the 
plaintiﬀ here seeks, were “in addition” to aĴorney’s fees and therefore do not include such fees. 
6 

RESPA contains a provision speciﬁcally providing for payment of an 
aĴorney’s fee incurred by a plaintiﬀ. Making an exception to the so-called 
American Rule obliging each party to litigation to bear its own legal expenses, 
section 2605(f)(3) requires a defendant that fails to comply with a RESPA 
requirement to pay a plaintiﬀ a reasonable aĴorney’s fee only “in the case of any 
successful action under this section [2605].” The plaintiﬀ has not prevailed in this 
action. 
Our dissenting colleague resists our conclusion, pointing out that “[the] 
canon [that the speciﬁc prevails over the general] gives a speciﬁc provision priority 
when two provisions cover the maĴer at issue.” Dissenting opinion 6. Here, the 
speciﬁc provision explicitly covers aĴorney’s fees, and, according to the dissent, 
the general provision on actual damages also covers, among other things, the 
aĴorney’s fees incurred in this case. The speciﬁc and general provisions, even on 
the dissent’s view, cover the same subject, and, if so, the speciﬁc provision controls. 
Finally, we consider the plaintiﬀ’s claim for $3.20, the cost of postage to send 
the second QWR. This claim fails under the venerable maxim “de minimis non 
curat lex” generally translated as “the law does not take account of triﬂes.” E.g., 
Sandifer v. U.S. Steel Corp., 571 U.S. 220, 233 (2014). 
7 

Our dissenting colleague counters that the de minimis doctrine does not 
apply here because RESPA sets a maximum limit on recoverable damages of 
$2,000. Dissenting opinion 7 (citing 12 U.S.C. § 2605(f)(1)(B)). We see no reason 
why a maximum on recoverable damages indicates that Congress wanted to 
burden federal courts with a de minimis claim of $3.20 for postage. See Ortiz v. 
NewRez LLC, 729 F. Supp. 3d 71, 74-75 (D. Mass. 2024) (claim for postage costs, 
incurred to send a second QWR after failure to fully comply with the ﬁrst QWR, 
disallowed as de minimis). 
Judgment aﬃrmed. 
25-2539-cv 
Murray v. Newrez LLC & PHH Mortgage Corporation 
1 

MYRNA PÉREZ, Circuit Judge, dissenting in part: 
 Sherry Ann Murray asked the servicers of her mortgage for information 
about her loan. They ignored her. Six weeks later, having received no 
acknowledgment or response, Murray tried again. For this second try, she paid 
an aĴorney $225 to prepare the requests and spent $3.20 to mail them. The 
majority opinion concludes that neither expense is recoverable under the Real 
Estate SeĴlement Procedures Act (“RESPA”), which permits borrowers to recover 
losses caused by a servicer’s failure to respond. The $225, it reasons, is an 
aĴorney’s fee recoverable only in a successful action, and Murray has not 
prevailed. And the $3.20 is too small to count. 
 I disagree with both conclusions. Paying an aĴorney to obtain a servicing 
response is not paying an aĴorney to litigate. And RESPA’s authorization of “any 
actual damages” contains no minimum dollar amount. See 12 U.S.C. 
§ 2605(f)(1)(A). Murray plausibly alleges that the servicers’ violations caused her 
to incur both expenses in seeking the response they were required to provide. 
Because I would permit that claim to proceed, I respectfully dissent. 
* * * 
 RESPA pairs a duty to respond with a remedy for failing to do so. When a 
servicer receives a qualiﬁed wriĴen request for information relating to the 
2 

servicing of a federally related mortgage loan, the statute generally requires a 
wriĴen acknowledgment within ﬁve business days and a response within the 
prescribed period. See 12 U.S.C. § 2605(e)(1)(A), (2); 12 C.F.R. § 1024.36(c)–(f). A 
servicer cannot simply ignore the request. Congress made a servicer that fails to 
provide the required acknowledgment or response liable for “any actual damages 
to the borrower as a result of the failure.” 12 U.S.C. § 2605(f)(1)(A). 
 Two features of that language guide the inquiry. First, the word “any” in 
“any actual damages” indicates breadth. See United States v. Gonzales, 520 U.S. 1, 5 
(1997). Congress did not limit recovery to particular categories of economic injury 
or impose a minimum dollar amount. The claimed expense must, of course, 
constitute an “actual” loss. 12 U.S.C. § 2605(f)(1)(A). But a real, out-of-pocket 
expense does not become any less actual because it is modest. 
 Second, “as a result of” requires a causal link between the violation and the 
expense. See Wirĵ v. Specialized Loan Servicing, LLC , 886 F.3d 713, 719 (8th Cir. 
2018); Renfroe v. Nationstar Mortg., LLC , 822 F.3d 1241, 1246 (11th Cir. 2016). The 
borrower must have incurred the expense because the servicer failed to comply, 
not merely after that failure. The connection must also be suﬃciently direct; a loss 
too remote from the violation does not qualify. See Lexmark Int’l, Inc. v. Static 
3 

Control Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118, 132 (2014) (“[W]e generally presume that a 
statutory cause of action is limited to plaintiﬀs whose injuries are proximately 
caused by violations of the statute.”). 
 Those causal requirements exclude much of what Murray seeks. I agree 
with the majority opinion that the interest and fees arising from her loan 
modiﬁcation do not constitute damages resulting from the servicing violations 
alleged here. The costs of preparing and sending her ﬁrst qualiﬁed wriĴen 
requests likewise are not recoverable because she incurred those costs before the 
servicers violated RESPA. The servicers’ later failure to respond could not have 
caused expenses Murray had already incurred. 
 The second requests, in my view, are diﬀerent. Murray alleges that the 
servicers’ failure to ackn

PER CURIAM 
 Plaintiff Aaron Kreiswirth appeals from a September 4, 2025 final 
judgment dismissing with prejudice his complaint in lieu of prerogative writs 
against defendants Planning Board of the Township of Lakewood (Board) and 
Sunset Road Sephardic Congregation, Inc. ( Sunset ). We affirm. 
 In April 2022, Sunset applied to the Board for preliminary and final major 
site plan approval of a two -story synagogue in Lakewood. Sunset's application 
sought variances for setback s to t he front, side, and rear yard s of the property 
and the number of parking spaces. Sunset 's proposed a building footprint of 
4,800 square feet foot , including a main sanctuary consisting of 2,900 square 
feet. 
 The Board held the first public hearing on Sunset 's application on May 23, 
2023. Plaintiff attended that hearing represented by counsel. In addition to the 
bulk variances, Sunset requested a variance for less than the thirty -seven parking 
spaces required by Lakewood Zoning Ordinance 18 -905 (Ordinance) . Plaintiff 's 

3 A-0031 -25 

attorney argued seventy -three parking spaces were required based on the total 
square footage of the proposed structure rather than the square footage of the 
main sanctuary . 
The Board heard testimony from Sunset 's professional engineer and 
planner , Brian Flannery. He testified the main sanctuary would total 2,900 
square feet. The Board 's engineer, Terence Vogt, calculated the main sanctuary 
would be 2,937 square feet. Flannery explained the parking would be the main 
issue with Sunset 's application . 
Regarding Sunset 's requested parking variance, the Board 's chairman 
advised that the discrepancy between the applicant 's proposed number of 
parking spaces and the required number of parking spaces under the Ordinance 
was significant and Sunset would "have to do a little better. " In response, 
Flannery told the Board that Sunset initially proposed more than six parking 
spaces on-site, but neighborhood residents requested a reduction in the number 
of parking spaces 
Flannery also addressed the other variances sought by Sunset, including a 
nine-foot rather than ten -foot side yard setback, a nineteen -foot rather than 
twenty-five-foot side yard setback, a five -foot rather than twenty -foot rear yard 
setback, 48% rather than 25% building coverage, and elimination of the twenty-

foot buffer requirement . Flannery testified these bulk variances could "be 
granted without substantial detriment to the public good. " 
On cross -examination by plaintiff 's attorney, Flannery did not know the 
number of congregants expected t o attend services at Sunset . Flannery 
maintained that "[a] 2,900 square foot main sanctuary requires [thirty -seven]

Plaintiff 's attorney then asked Flannery "[i]f you have a property where 
there's a main sanctuary for men and a main sanctuary for women, how do you

has been applied for [forty] years. " 
The Board 's chairman suggested Sunset may have to return to the Board 
with a plan for additional parking. The Board 's attorney explained "[t]he 
applicant has the right to put their case on and make all their proofs and the 
Board can decide the final. The Chairman certainly has the right, though, to 
limit the testimony and limit the cross examination, get to the point ." Based on 
counsel 's statement, t he Board 's chairman precluded further cross -examination 
of Sunset 's planner related to parking.

The hearing proceeded with testimony from plaintiff. Plaintiff, who lived 
next to the proposed synagogue, testified the area lacked adequate parking , and 
the application would result in "parking across the sidewalk " daily. Plaintiff 
stated he observed six cars "on a regular basis that frequent this property. " 
Plaintiff 's attorney introduced photographs taken by plaintiff showing cars 
parked on the road near the proposed synagogue . However, plaintiff could not 
confirm the cars in the photographs belonged to members of the synagogue. 
Sunset next called Rabbi Moshe Waddische to testify in favor of the 
application. The r abbi told the Board members the congregation consistently 
had sixty -six members paying members who attended services . Regarding 
parking, the rabbi stated Sunset presently had three or four cars parking on the 
existing driveway. T he rabbi testified "we have about [fifteen] people coming 
and they 're, basically, from the area and they park. That 's not an issue. Now, 
in the evening we have some more people there, sometimes [twenty] or [thirty] 
people. They live closer. They 're able to park. When it 's [thirty] people, they 
take up . . . the entire Sunset [Road]. " 

6 A-0031 -25 

On cross -examination, plaintiff 's attorney asked the rabbi about the use of 
a back room to be connected to the main sanctuary . The rabbi responded the 
back room could be used as an overflow room for men attending services. 1 
 The r abbi confirmed the upstairs section of the proposed synagogue 
served "as a women 's sanctuary " and only about three or four women attended 
services on the Sabbath . He further explained the upstairs sanctuary could

A Board member then asked the r abbi if Sunset could acquire additional

The Board continued the public hearing on September 19, 2023. Before 
this meeting, Sunset submitted revised plans based on comments during t he

Flannery presented additional parking testimony at this hearing . He

A Board member asked if there was a signed agreement with the shopping

So, it 's not signed. It 's subject to, obviously, approval. 
I have no problem providing, as we 've done in the past 
on other applications, should the Board vote in favor

reviewing the agreement. There is a draft of it. There 
is an easement agreement. I have no problem sharing

 Flannery testified the Township 's off -site parking ordinance allows 
applicants to "provide the parking on another parcel which may or may not be

and [where the applicant] provides assurances acceptable to the appropriate

 Plaintiff 's attorney challenged the required number of parking spaces,

Plaintiff 's attorney then argued the shopping center was encumbered by a

The Board 's chairman responded the Township 's engineer would "look[] at these

The Board held a final public hearing on December 5, 2023. At this

 Sunset presented testimony from Scott Kennel, a traffic expert. Kennel 
reviewed the parking at the shopping center . He estimated fifty parking spaces

examination, p laintiff 's attorney asked Kennel, "if there 's more than one

Sunset 's counsel objected , stating : 
[W]e went through this at length. The ordinance in

leads.caseName: CLINTON NALLEY v. CARROLL COUNTY
leads.text:
SECOND DIVISION
 DOYLE, P. J.,
 DAVIS and WHITAKER, JJ.

 NOTICE: Motions for reconsideration must be
 received no later than 4:30 pm on the 10th day after
 the decision was issued to be deemed timely filed.
 https://www.gaappeals.gov/rules

 November 2, 2026

In the Court of Appeals of Georgia
 A26A1562. NALLEY et al. v. CARROLL COUNTY.

 DOYLE, Presiding Judge.

 Clinton Nalley, Amberly Nalley, The Barn at Nalley Properties, LLC, and

Nalley Properties, LLC (collectively, the “Nalleys”) filed a complaint against Carroll

County seeking a declaratory judgment that a conditional use permit (“CUP”)

previously issued for one of their properties automatically extends to cover a different

piece of property that they subsequently acquired. The parties filed cross-motions for

summary judgment, and after a hearing, the trial court granted Carroll County’s

motion and denied the Nalleys’ motion. The Nalleys appealed, arguing that the trial

court erred by denying their motion for summary judgment because (1) the previously

issued CUP extended as a matter of law to the newly acquired piece of property; and
 (2) the Nalleys acquired vested rights by virtue of the County Planner’s purported

assurances that the previously issued CUP would extend to cover the newly acquired

piece of property. For the reasons that follow, we affirm.

 “On appeal from the grant or denial of summary judgment, we conduct a de

novo review, with all reasonable inferences construed in the light most favorable to the

nonmoving party.” Sterling Planet, Inc. v. GRP Holdco, LLC, 374 Ga. App. 754 (913

SE2d 881) (2025) (quotation marks omitted). Additionally, the construction of a

zoning ordinance is a question of law, which we review de novo. See Sprayberry v. Bd.

of Comm’rs. of Putnam County, 366 Ga. App. 810, 810-11 (884 SE2d 429) (2023).

 So viewed, the record reflects that in February 2016, the Nalleys purchased a

15-acre tract of land in Carroll County, on which they currently live. A 2018 plat of

survey divided their 15-acre parcel into two separate parcels — a 5-acre parcel

including a barn as an event venue and a 10-acre parcel on which their home is located.

In June 2019, they applied for a CUP allowing them to use the five-acre parcel as a

special events venue to host weddings and parties. In August 2019, the Carroll County

Board of Commissioners approved the CUP application, allowing use of the property

as a small special events facility.

 Relevant to this appeal, Section 102-4 of Carroll County’s Zoning Code of

 2
 Ordinances provides as follows:

 Conditional use means a use for a particular piece of property that
 may be allowed by the Governing Authority when specifically listed in
 and provided for by this ordinance. A conditional use is subject to such
 restrictive requirements as in the opinion of the Governing Authority
 would be necessary to insure that the use is not detrimental to
 surrounding property. ...

 Special events facility shall mean any place kept, used, maintained,
 advertised, or held out to the public as a place which serves as a location
 for special events including, but not limited to, weddings and receptions,
 ... and other similar parties, receptions, or events. Such facility includes
 privately-owned properties which have existing agricultural structures
 such as barns or outdoor agricultural areas such as lakes, open pastures,
 or fields, where such special events may take place and that can be
 maintained as or converted back to agricultural structures or areas. Such
 facility shall be open only for scheduled, event-based operations. Such
 facility shall not include places of worship or restaurants. No such facility
 shall be closer than 50 feet from a property line. There shall be three
 categories of special events facilities as follows:

 (1) “Small special events facility” shall mean a special event
 facility with a maximum event size of 150 guests and shall be located on
 a minimum parcel size of four acres or larger.

 (2) “Intermediate special events facility” shall mean a special
 event facility with a maximum event size of 250 guests and shall be

 3
  located on a minimum parcel size of 25 acres or larger.

 (3) “Large special events facility” shall mean a special event
 facility with a maximum event size of 500 guests and shall be located on
 a minimum parcel of 50 acres or larger.

 Additionally, Section 102-12.9 of Carroll County’s Zoning Code of Ordinances

sets forth the procedures for determining whether to grant a CUP, including a

requirement that the applicant must submit “a current boundary survey and plat plan

... [or] other similar drawing, sketch, or plans that properly identifies the boundaries

of the planned development[,]” and a public hearing before the Carroll County Board

of Commissioners, which is required to consider 13 specific factors regarding the

potential adverse effects of granting a CUP on the area in which the proposed use will

be located.

 In 2021, the Nalleys became interested in purchasing a neighboring 15.67-acre

property, on which a climate controlled barn is located, for purposes of hosting

weddings and other events. The 15.67-acre property, which is zoned agricultural, is

contiguous with the eastern border of the 10-acre tract on which the Nalleys’

residence is located but is not contiguous to the western 5-acre tract to which the 2019

CUP applies.

 4
  In August 2021, Clint Nalley spoke over the phone with Janet Hyde, the county

planner, regarding the proposed purchase of the 15.67-acre property. Clint testified

that the substance of this conversation was as follows:

 [S]o I then called Janet Hyde at the County and I asked — I told her, I
 said, this is Clint Nalley, Barn at Nalley Properties, and we’re looking at
 purchasing the property next to us and what amendments would need to
 be made in order for us to extend that permit to purchase this property
 and combine the parcel, and she said, none, as long as you stay under the
 25 acres, and that was the end of that conversation.

Clint testified that during this conversation he did not mention to Hyde that the

Nalleys wanted to host weddings and other events on the property. Also in August

2021, Aaron McCullough, a surveyor engaged by the Nalleys, had a phone

conversation with Hyde in which he inquired generally as to the parameters of

expanding a conditional use permit, and Hyde responded that the two situations in

which an existing CUP required modification were “if an existing facility’s property

exceeded 25 acres in aggregate or ... if new buildings were constructed on the

property.”1

 Thereafter, the Nalleys entered into a purchase agreement for the 15.67-acre

 1
 Hyde’s recollection of her conversations with Clint and McCullough was
never preserved via testimony or affidavit, and she passed away during the pendency
of the litigation.
 5
 property. Prior to closing, the Nalleys applied to formally combine the 5-acre property

and the 15.67-acre property into a single parcel. In December 2021, McCullough e-

mailed Hyde a “preliminary reconfiguration”2 of the two properties, informing her

of the Nalleys’ intention to purchase the 15.67-acre property and asking,

“Conceptually, is this approvable?” Hyde responded in the affirmative. On December

15, 2021, the Nalleys closed on their purchase of the 15.67-acre property for $1.2

million. On December 22, 2021, Hyde approved the Nalleys’ application to combine

the parcels, the combined acreage of which now totaled 20.67.3

 In 2022, after expending substantial amounts for improvements of the newly

acquired property, the Nalleys began hosting weddings on the property and

advertising it as a special event venue. Hyde thereafter informed the Nalleys that the

2019 CUP did not extend to the newly acquired property and that the Nalleys would

need to apply for a separate CUP for the property to hold weddings and other such

 2
 The preliminary configuration depicted a 20.67-acre area including the
western 5-acre parcel to which the CUP applied and the yet-to-be-purchased 15.67-
acre parcel to the east of the 10-acre parcel on which the Nalleys lived as Tract I. The
Nalleys’ 10-acre residential property was represented as Tract II. A narrow, L-shaped
strip of land running along the northwest corner and northern border of Tract II
connecting the 5- and 15.67-acre parcels was also depicted.
 3
 The strip of land running along the northwest corner and northern border of
the Nalleys’ 10-acre residential property as depicted in the preliminary configuration
now connected the 5- and 15.67-acre parcels.
 6
 events there. In March 2022, the Nalleys submitted an application for a CUP for the

newly acquired property. In May 2022, the Carroll County Board of Commissioners

denied the application.

 In June 2022, the Nalleys filed a complaint against Carroll County, the Carroll

County Board of Commissioners, and its individual members, in which they petitioned

for a writ of certiorari as to the decision to deny their CUP application and requested

declaratory relief. However, in January 2025, pursuant to State v. Sass Group, LLC,

315 Ga. 893 (885 SE2d 761) (2023), the trial court dismissed the Nalleys’ original

complaint without prejudice because it had named both Carroll County and the

individual members of the Carroll County Board of Commissioners as defendants.

The Nalleys thereafter brought a renewal complaint pursuant to OCGA § 9-2-61(a)

against Carroll County only, in which they sought a declaratory judgment that the

2019 CUP previously applicable to their 5-acre parcel of property automatically

extends to cover the newly acquired 15.67-acre parcel and, alternatively, that Hyde’s

representations regarding the purchase and combination of the new property with the

5-acre parcel resulted in the Nalleys’ vested right to use the new property as a

wedding venue without a CUP.

 Discovery ensued, and eventually the Nalleys and Carroll County filed cross-

 7
 motions for summary judgment. The trial court convened a hearing on the parties’

motions, thereafter entering an order denying the Nalleys’ motion and granting

Carroll County’s motion. In its order, the trial court ruled that Carroll County’s

approval of the Nalleys’ application to combine the 5-acre parcel to which the 2019

CUP applied with the subsequently acquired 15.67-acre parcel did not automatically

extend the 2019 CUP to the subsequently acquired land. Additionally, the trial court

noted that allowing the Nalleys to bypass applicable zoning ordinances in this way

would deprive Carroll County of the opportunity to assess the impact of the proposed

change in land use on the surrounding area. The Nalleys filed an application for

discretionary appeal, which this Court granted, and this appeal followed.

 1. The Nalleys contend that the trial court erred by declining to issue a

declaratory judgment that the 2019 CUP applicable to their 5-acre parcel extends as

a matter of law to cover the newly acquired 15.67-acre parcel. In particular, they argue

that this result should follow from the fact that Carroll County’s zoning code does not

expressly prohibit it. We disagree.

 “[Z]oning ordinances should be strictly construed in favor of the property

owner, and ambiguities in the language of zoning ordinances should be resolved in

favor of the free use of property. At the same time, [this Court] give[s] local

 8
 ordinances a reasonable construction where possible.” Bd. of Comm’rs of Henry

County v. Welch, 253 Ga. 682, 683(1) (324 SE2d 178) (1985) (cleaned up). “[A]ll parts

of an ordinance relating to the same subject matter must be harmonized to reconcile

conflicts, and any section of an ordinance must be construed in relation to the whole

ordinance of which it is part.” SDS Real Prop. Holdings, Ltd. v. City of Brookhaven, 341

Ga. App. 862, 866(1) (802 SE2d 100) (2017) (quotation marks omitted).

 The te
