SUPERIOR COURT OF NEW JERSEY 
 APPELLATE DIVISION 
 DOCKET NO . A-2520-24 

637 ARNOLD, LLC , 

 Plaintiff -Appellant, 

v. 

ARNOLD SHORES, LLC, 
HOLLSTON HILLS, LLC, 
HOLLSTON REALTY GROUP, 
LLC, BOROUGH OF POINT 
PLEASANT BEACH , and 
BOROUGH OF POINT 
PLEASANT BEACH ZONING 
BOARD OF ADJUSTMENT, 
jointly and severally , 

 Defendant s-Respondents. 
____________________________ 

Argued September 28, 2026 – Decided October 30, 2026 

Before Judges Sabatino and Torregrossa -O'Connor. 

On appeal from the Superior Court of New Jersey, Law 
Division, Ocean County, Docket No. L -2077-24. 

Ryan J. Murphy argued the cause for appellant (Gertner 
Murphy LLC, attorneys; Ryan J. Murphy , of counsel 
and on the brief s). 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION WITHOUT THE 
APPROVAL OF THE APPELLATE DIVISION 

This opinion shall not "constitute precedent or be binding upon any court ." Although it is posted on the 
internet , this opinion is binding only on the parties in the case and its use in other cases is limited . R. 1:36 -3. 

2 A-2520 -24 

John J. Jackson, III argued the cause for respondents 
Arnold Shores, LLC, Hollston Hills, LLC and Hollston 
Realty Group, LLC ( John J. Jackson III & Associates, 
Attorneys at Law , LLC, attorneys; John J. Jackson , III, 
of counsel and on the brief; Jilian McLeer, on the brief). 

Ben A. Montenegro argued the cause for respondent 
Borough of Point Pleasant Beach Zoning Board of 
Adjustment (Montenegro Thompson Montenegro & 
Genz, attorneys; Ben A. Montenegro and Ryan M. 
Amberger , on the brief ). 

PER CURIAM 
 This zoning appeal arises from site plan approvals and variance relief 
granted for renovation of the historic Gottlieb Building (the property ) located in 
the downtown commercial district of the Borough of Point Pleasant Beach (the 
Borough) . Specifically, t he Borough Zoning Board of Adjustment ( the Board) 
unanimously approved a project permitting mixed use of the two -story building 
and allowing construction of a restaurant and spa on the first level and a seven-
room hotel on the second floor (the project) . 
Plaintiff 637 Arnold, LLC , a neighboring property owner and objector to 
the project , sharing a common lot line with the property , now appeal s from the 
March 7, 2025 Law Division order dismissing with prejudice plaintiff's 
complaint in lieu of prerogative writs which it filed against the Board , the 
Borough, and the owners of the subject property, Arnold Shores, LLC, Hollston 

3 A-2520 -24 

Hills, LLC, and Hollston Realty Group, LLC (collectively Gottlieb defendants) ,1 
seeking reversal of the Board's approval . We have reviewed the record in light 
of applicable legal principles, and we affirm substantially for the detailed 
reasons stated by Judge Francis R. Hodgson , Jr., A.J.S.C., in his cogent oral 
decision accompanying the March 7 order, and his well-reasoned nineteen -page 
May 9, 2025 amplification of decision , provided pursuant to Rule 2:5-1(d). 
I. 
A. 
The following summary suffices to set forth the salient facts and 
procedural history pertinent to this appea l. Notably, t his was not the first zoning 
application approved by the Board to revitalize the Gottlieb Building, erected in 
1906 and located at 641 Arnold Avenue . In 2020 , prior to the Gottlieb 
defendants ' application , the property's previous owners sought , and in 2021 
obtained , variance relief to construct a first -floor marketplace and second -floor 

1 At all relevant times , defendants Arnold Shores, LLC, Hollston Hills, LLC, 
and Hollston Realty Group, LLC , acted jointly in furtherance of the application . 
Arnold Shores, LLC owns the property. "Business Entry Status Reports " for 
these entities contained in the record reflect that Arnold Shores, LLC's agent 
and principal is Hollston Hills, LLC. Don Slaght testified at the Board hearing, 
explaining he is the "principal [of] Hollston Hills, LLC, which is the managing 
member of Arnold Shores, LLC ." Thus, for clarity, we reference these 
defendants collectively as the Gottlieb defendants, the manner in which they 
were often jointly identified in the record and briefing. 

4 A-2520 -24 

hotel within the building , but never commenc ed the work. Plaintiff also 
unsuccessfu lly opposed th at earlier application. Here, the Gottlieb defendants 
sought variance relief pursuant to N.J.S.A. 40:55D -70(d)(1) and (2) and 
included new plans for the restaurant and spa . The proposed project retained in 
all respects the prior approved plan for the second -floor hotel . Thus, for context, 
we briefly review the 2020 application and approvals. 
The prior owners, then -represented by now-counsel for t he Gottlieb 
defendants , sought site plan approval and d(1) and bulk variances to "renovate 
and construct a[n] . . . addition to an existing commercial building" as well as 
"expand existing retail use and convert the upper levels to a hotel use on the 
property known as 641 Arnold Avenue." The prior application relied upon a 
January 23, 2019 survey of the land. The Board approved a d(1) variance, 
finding : the site to be "particularly suited" for the proposed use; the application 
met "the purposes of zoning . . . by promoting the public health, safety, morals, 
and general welfare"; "the proposed use w [ould] have no substantial negative 
impact on the surrounding property owners"; and "the relief sought d [id] not 
impair the intent and purpose of the Master Plan or Zoning Ordinance of the 
Borough." The resolution specifically granted d(1) variance approval for the 
hotel, which is not otherwise a permitted use in th at commercial zone. 

5 A-2520 -24 

As in the present matter , plaintiff then filed a n unsuccessful prerogative 
writs action in Superior Court seeking to reverse the Board's approval of the 
project . A prior judge upheld the Board's determination and dismissed the 
complaint. In 2023, the prior owners , having not moved forward with the 
approved project, sold the property to the Gottlieb defendants . 
Related to the 2020 application, Judge Hodgson , in an action addressing 
an apparent "boundary line dispute" pertaining to the property, "ordered the 
parties to proceed by commissioners pursuant to N.J.S.A. 2A:28 -1 et seq."2 The 
commissioners ' report corrected the property's common boundary line with 
plaintiff's property and included a new boundary line description and plat, but 
indicat ed they "[did] not attempt[] to determine if any of the structures on [the 
parties' lots] overlap the boundary line." On June 11, 2021, Judge Hodgson 
entered a "final order in th[e] matter" directing that "[t]he boundary line defined 

2 N.J.S.A. 2A:28 -1 directs: 

When any dispute arises between the owners of 
adjoining lands as to the location of any dividing line 
or lines between such lands, the Superior Court may, on 
application of either owner on notice to the other, 
appoint three disinterested commissioners, one of 
whom shall be a practical surveyor, who shall fix, 
ascertain and regulate such lines. 

6 A-2520 -24 

in the [c]ommissioner[s'] report shall be considered to have conclusively 
established the boundary line between the subject properties ." 
B. 
 In 2024, Arnold Shores filed its application for approval of a new 
integrated use of the property. It sought approval to retain the identical plan for 
the upstairs hotel, with a newly -proposed first-floor use to permit construction 
of a restaurant —a permitted use, and a spa—a non-permitted use . Public notice 
of the application followed , which advised : "Arnold Shores[,] LLC has applied 
to the [Board] for amended site plan approval and for any required use variance 
to allow the street level to be used as a restaurant in one section and a spa in 
another section where the second floor will be occupied by a p reviously 
approved non -conforming hotel use. " The notice included the date and location 
of the hearing, the specific address of the project, including lot and block 
number, and a description of the nature of the project . It disclosed that d(1) and 
d(2) "variances and[] design waivers" were sought, including use variances for 
the hotel and the spa, and also notified of the right to appear with questions or 
objections and the available means and manner to inspect the applica tion prior 
to the hearing. . 

7 A-2520 -24 

 The Board held three public hearings related to the application: March 7, 
2024; April 4, 2024; and May 30, 2024. Plaintiff appeared as an objector 
throughout the proceedings. The Board preliminarily addressed and rejected 
plaintiff's written and oral objections to the notice, and the Gottlieb defendants 
presented testimony over the various hearing dates from their manager, 
architect, licensed professional planner , and one of the owners . Over the course 
of the hearings, the Gottlieb defendants voluntarily submitted a revised site plan 
to both address certain concerns raised by neighbors and the Board about various 
aspects of the project and to reflect an updated survey incorporat ing the 2020 
correction of the boundary line with plaintiff's property. 
 At the conclusion of the testimony, the Board unanimously approved the 
application. On June 20, 2024, it issued a resolution memorializing the 
approval. After summarizing all the hearing evidence, the resolution expressly 
stated the Board found the Gottlieb defendants ' planner persuasive , and accepted 
and adopt ed the planner's testimony and conclusions concerning the project . 
The resolution , at time s citing directly to the planner's testimony, found the 
application: "met the requirements of N.J.S.A. 40:55D -70(d)(1) because the 
Board determined that the site is particularly suitable for this site " and "the 
proposed uses, . . . will be an attractive addition to the Arnold Avenue 

8 A-2520 -24 

downtown while providing vitality and convenience of multiple uses to area 
residents and visitors "; "the applicant has met the requirements of N.J.S.A. 
40:55D -70(d)(2) "; "the relief sought (with conditions imposed) can be granted 
without a substantial negative impact to the public good "; and "the relief sought 
(with conditions imposed) does not impair the intent and purpose of the Master 
Plan or Zoning Ordinance of the Borough of Point Pleasant Beach ." 
C. 
 On August 12, 2024, plaintiff filed its complaint in lieu of prerogative 
writs seeking reversal of the Board's approval. All defendants answered , and 
the Borough filed a motion to dismiss the complaint. Plaintiff moved to 
disqualify the Gottlieb defendants' counsel as a potential witness . The 
prerogative writ s trial was set for March 7, 2025. 
At the trial, plaintiff argued various alleged flaws in the zoning procedures 
and approvals necessitate d the court's reversing the Board. Summarized 
succinctly, plaintiff alleged : public notice was deficient because the description 
of the application failed to enumerate the correct variances required for the 
project ; the Board was required to , but did not , address the need for a d(1) 
variance for the integrated use of the property for restaurant, spa, and hotel, 
applied the incorrect legal standard, and improperly relied on prior approvals as 

9 A-2520 -24 

the multi -use project changed substantially from the 2020 plan for which 
approval was granted; the site plan was invalid as it relied upon an invalidated 
survey; the Board failed to consider public health and safety concerns related to 
building code violations ; the Board usurped the role of the governing body and 
permitted a new use by approving the "boutique hotel" without proper authority; 
and the Board and the Gottlieb defendants ' counsel were biased , tainting the 
proceedings . 
 Defendants countered that the notice was clear and adequate , and the 
amended site plan addressed any issues regarding the relatively insignificant 
changes to the boundary lines in the amended survey . They argued the Board 
properly addressed the requ

SUPERIOR COURT OF NEW JERSEY 
 APPELLATE DIVISION

v. 

CARLTON WILLIAMS -SEWELL 
and JOYCE PETERS ,

Submitted October 22, 2026 – Decided October 30, 2026 

Before Judges Chase and Augostini. 

On appeal from the Superior Court of New Jersey, Law 
Division , Camden County , Docket No. DC -009679 -25. 

Giordano, Halleran & Ciesla, P C, attorneys for 
appellant (Steven W. Ward , on the briefs). 

Carlton Williams -Sewell and Joyce Peters, self -

PER CURIAM

APPROVAL OF THE APPELLATE DIVISION 

This opinion shall not "constitute precedent or be binding upon any court ." Although it is posted on the 
internet , this opinion is binding only on the parties in the case and its use in other cases is limited . R. 1:36 -3. 

2 A-0801 -25 

Plaintiff Lakeview Realty Investment Associates, LP (Lakeview) appeals 
from a Special Civil Part order granting summary judgment to defendants 
Carlton Williams -Sewell and Joyce Peters. We vacate and remand . 
In February 2024, Lakeview filed a landlord -tenant complaint seeking 
possession of residential premises in Blackwood based on nonpayment of rent. 
On April 9, 2024, the parties entered into a consent agreement. The agreement 
provided in relevant part: 
1. The Tenant agrees to the immediate entry of 
Judgment for Possession and that the Warrant of 
Removal may issue and be served upon the Tenant at 
the Landlord 's request, as permitted by law, The 
Landlord agrees that the warrant of removal cannot be 
executed (no eviction) until [April 30, 2024] , ( "the 
move out date "), unless the Tenant fails to comply with 
[p]aragraph 2(b). 

2. The Tenant shall pay no money. Any possession 
remaining shall be considered abandoned. Defendant 
will return keys . 

3. a. If the Tenant does not make all payments required 
in [p]aragraph 2( [b]) of this Agreement , the Tenant 
agrees that the Landlord, with notice to the Tenant, can 
file a certification stating when and wha t the breach was 
and that that the warrant of removal can then be 
executed upon, as permitted by law , prior to the agreed 
upon move out date. [1] 

1 Paragraph 1 and paragraph 3(a) refer to "paragraph 2(b), " but the agreement 
contains no paragraph 2(b). This appears to be a drafting error . 

3 A-0801 -25 

That same day, the court entered a judgment for possession by consent. 
 On May 23, 2025, Lakeview filed this separate Special Civil Part action 
to recover unpaid rent that had accrued before the parties signed the consent 
agreement. Williams -Sewell responded by filing a copy of the consent 
agreement from the landlord -tenant matter. The court treated the filing as an 
answer and scheduled trial for September 2, 2025 . 
In August 2025, Lakeview moved for summary judgment, arguing 
defendants had filed no contesting answer. Lakeview also requested an 
adjournment of the trial pending disposition of that motion. The court denied 
the adjournment request. 
The parties appeared for trial on September 2, 2025. On the record, the 
court dismissed the complaint because it interpreted the consent agreement as 
waiving Lakeview 's right to recover any rent arrears from defendants. The court 
did not enter a written order that day. 
Ten days later, the court entered an order granting Lakeview 's motion for 
summary judgment. Around the same time, Lakeview moved for 
reconsideration of the court 's oral dismissal. A few days later, defendants 
moved to vacate the summary judgment order. 

4 A-0801 -25 

On October 15, 2025, the court entered an order denying Lakeview 's 
reconsideration motion. That same day, the court denied defendants ' motion to 
vacate the summary judgment order as moot. 
In November 2025, Lakeview filed a notice of appeal from the oral 
dismissal and the order denying reconsideration. The Appellate Clerk 's office 
informed Lakeview its appeal could not proceed because no written dismissal 
order had been entered. Lakeview then asked the trial court to issue one. On 
December 5, 2025, the court entered an order memorializing its earlier oral 
dismissal. 
 "A trial court 's interpretation of the law and the legal consequences that 
flow from established facts are not entitled to any special deference. " Rowe v. 
Bell & Gossett Co. , 239 N.J. 531, 552 (2019) (quoting Manalapan Realty, L.P. 
v. Twp. Comm. of Manalapan , 140 N.J. 366, 378 (1995)). The interpretation 
and construction of a settlem ent agreement is a matter of law for the trial court, 
subject to de novo review on appeal. Kaur v. Assured Lending Corp., 405 N.J. 
Super. 468, 474 (App. Div. 2009) (citing Spring Creek Holding Co. v. Shinnihon 
U.S.A. Co., 399 N.J. Super. 158, 190 (App. Div. 2008)) . 
 Lakeview argues the trial court misread the consent agreement. 
According to Lakeview, the agreement relieved defendants only of any 

5 A-0801 -25 

obligation to pay additional rent between April 9, 2024, and the agreed move -
out date of April 30, 2024. Lakeview contends the agreement did not waive its 
right to pursue unpaid rent accrued before April 9, 2024. 
Under our summary di spossess statute, landlords may elect an expedited 
procedure to regain possession of leased premises in the event of non-payment 
of rent. N.J.S.A. 2A:18 -53(b). But the Special Civil Part has limited jurisdiction 
in landlord -tenant cases . It adjudicates possession, not money damages . Hodges 
v. Sasil Corp. , 189 N.J. 210 , 221 (2007) (citing Hous. Auth. of Morristown v. 
Little, 135 N.J. 274, 28 0 (1994)). As the Court has explained, "[p]ossession of 
the premises is the only available remedy for non payment of rent, because 
money damages may not be awarded in a summary dispossess action. " Ibid. A 
landlord seeking unpaid rent therefore must file a separate action. 
Read in that context, the consent agreement did not waive Lakeview 's 
claim for rent arrears that predated the agreement. Paragraph 2 states "[t]he 
Tenant shall pay no money. " This means defendants did not have to pay 
additional money to remain in possession through the agreed move -out date. 
This language does not clearly release defendants from liability for rent already 
due under the lease before the parties signed the agreement. 

6 A-0801 -25 

The consent agreement reflects Lakeview did not require defendants to 
pay any money for allowing them to remain at the property from the three weeks 
between the consent agreement and the eviction date. And because the landlord -
tenant action could resolve only possession, not damages, Lakeview had no 
occasion in that proceeding to seek a money judgment for unpaid rent. Its failure 
to reserve expressly the right to bring a later collection action did not amount to 
a waiver of that right. 
The consideration recited in the agreement reinforces these conclusions . 
Lakeview agreed to delay execution of the warrant of removal until April 30, 
2024, and defendants, in turn, agreed to vacate and return the keys. The "no 
money" language addressed that brief post -agreement period of continued 
occupancy. Again, it did not extinguish liability for unpaid rent that had accrued 
earlier. 
Accordingly, the trial court was mistaken in construing the consent 
agreement as barring this action for unpaid rent. We therefore vacate the 
summary judgment order and remand for a trial on the merits. 
Vacated and remanded . We do not retain jurisdiction.

leads.caseName: Lampton Securities Partnership, LLP v. Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government
leads.text:
RENDERED: OCTOBER 30, 2026; 10:00 A.M.
 TO BE PUBLISHED

 Commonwealth of Kentucky
 Court of Appeals
 NO. 2025-CA-1380-MR

LAMPTON SECURITIES
PARTNERSHIP, LLP APPELLANT

 APPEAL FROM JEFFERSON CIRCUIT COURT
v. HONORABLE JESSICA E. GREEN, JUDGE
 ACTION NO. 20-CI-003017

LOUISVILLE-JEFFERSON COUNTY
METRO GOVERNMENT AND
METROPOLITAN SEWER DISTRICT APPELLEES

 OPINION
 AFFIRMING

 ** ** ** ** **

BEFORE: COMBS, EASTON, AND L. JONES, JUDGES.

JONES, L., JUDGE: Lampton Securities Partnership (Lampton) appeals from the

Jefferson Circuit Court’s order granting summary judgment to Louisville-Jefferson

County Metro Government (Metro Government) and the Metropolitan Sewer

District (Metro Sewer) in this reverse condemnation action. We affirm.
  In the early 1990s, the owners of a roughly four-acre tract along the

Ohio River received approval from Metro Sewer to construct condominiums. The

plan approved by Metro Sewer contained two phases of construction.1 Though it is

uncontested that the owners received approval of the plan, the actual permit is not

in the record. Phase One was completed on roughly two acres. The remaining two

1
 Metro Government and Metro Sewer seem to dispute both phases were approved. But the
deposition testimony of Metro Sewer’s designated representative indicates that both were
approved:

 Q. Okay. So [Metro Sewer] approved the construction plans—

 A. Yeah, that was back in ’92.

 Q. Back in ’92. Okay. And do you recall what those plans
 entailed?

 A. They showed a condo, a large condo complex. It had a Phase 1
 and a Phase 2. Phase 1 was the only one that was built.

 Q. Right. But both phases were approved.

 A. They were both shown on the plan.

 Q. They were both shown on the plan.

 A. (Nods head affirmatively)

 Q. It was a total of four acres, and that was the development that
 was approved by [Metro Sewer] in 1992 or ’93, correct?

 A. ’92, yes.

 Q. In ’92. So there is no question that [Metro Sewer] approved
 the development of both tracts of land in 1992, correct?

 A. It appeared to be a single tract on the plans that we have.

Trial Court Record (TR) at 628.

 -2-
 acres (Tract) were the planned location for Phase Two. A building to house

electrical equipment was erected on the Tract, and utility lines were put in place.

However, no condominiums were built on the Tract.

 Meanwhile, in 1997, the Metro Government enacted floodplain

ordinances in response to catastrophic flooding. Essentially, the ordinances

prevent most types of new construction on land within the “conveyance zone”

portion of the floodplain. The Tract is within the conveyance zone.

 However, the ordinances have two relevant exceptions. First, they

permit the continuation of construction which had already begun before the

ordinances were adopted. Second, an impacted landowner is permitted to seek a

variance from Metro Sewer’s Floodplain Board (Board).2 The record contains

evidence of variances the Board has granted to other landowners.

2
 In relevant part, § 157.03(A)(1) provides that “[n]o development . . . shall occur in the local
regulatory conveyance zone except as approved in a permit issued by the administering agency”
but subsection (C)(8) allows the continuation of a nonconforming use “which was lawful on the
effective date of this chapter . . . .” Ordinance § 157.04(B) provides that the Board “may grant”
a “specific variance from the individual provisions of § 157.03 . . . .”

 Metro Government’s official website contains a hyperlink leading to the American Legal
Publishing Company’s website, where the entirety of local ordinances and code provisions may
be viewed. See https://louisvilleky.gov/government/codes-regulations/local-ordinances (last
visited Oct. 2, 2026). The ordinances quoted above thus may be viewed at
https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/louisvillemetro/latest/loukymetro/0-0-0-
17164#JD_157.03 (last visited Oct. 2, 2026). We used the same method to view another
municipality’s ordinances in Schell v. Young, 640 S.W.3d 24, 30 n.2 (Ky. App. 2021).

 -3-
  In 1998, after the enactment of the floodplain ordinances, Lampton

purchased the Tract for $800,000.00. The Tract sat idle until Lampton placed it on

the market around 2019. The marketing materials asserted that the Tract could be

commercially developed. Metro Sewer personnel somehow learned the Tract was

for sale and a meeting eventually occurred between Metro Sewer’s counsel and

Lampton. At that meeting, Metro Sewer’s counsel opined that the floodplain

ordinances prevented development of the Tract.

 Lampton neither sought a variance nor attempted to begin the

construction of Phase Two (in reliance upon the previously granted permit).

Instead, in May 2020, Lampton filed this reverse condemnation action against

Metro Sewer and Metro Government. The complaint asserts Lampton “lost all

economically beneficial uses” of the Tract because of the enactment and

enforcement of the floodplain ordinances. TR at 9.

 After protracted discovery and vigorous motion practice, the trial

court granted summary judgment to Metro Sewer and Metro Government in July

2025. Though the parties had raised additional arguments, the trial court’s

decision was based on two conclusions. First, the court concluded that Lampton

had failed to exhaust its administrative remedies. Second, the court concluded the

complaint had not been timely filed. After the court denied its motion to alter,

amend, or vacate, Lampton filed this appeal.

 -4-
  Kentucky’s familiar summary judgment standards are:

 In considering a motion for summary judgment, a
 trial court must view the record in a light most favorable
 to the non-moving party, resolving all doubts in its favor.
 Steelvest, Inc. v. Scansteel Serv. Ctr., Inc., 807 S.W.2d
 476, 480 (Ky. 1991). The trial court may grant summary
 judgment only if it concludes that no disputed issues of
 material fact exist for trial. Id. On appeal of a summary
 judgment, we must determine whether the trial court
 correctly found that the moving party was entitled to a
 judgment as a matter of law. Id. Because summary
 judgment involves questions of law, we need not defer to
 the trial court’s conclusions; accordingly, we review the
 record de novo. Blevins v. Moran, 12 S.W.3d 698, 700-
 01 (Ky. App. 2000).

Waugh v. Parker, 584 S.W.3d 748, 750–51 (Ky. 2019).

 Of course, under settled Kentucky precedent, “[i]f an appellate court

is aware of a reason to affirm the lower court’s decision, it must do so, even if on

different grounds.” Mark D. Dean, P.S.C. v. Commonwealth Bank & Tr. Co., 434

S.W.3d 489, 496 (Ky. 2014) (emphasis added). Pursuant to that principle, after

examining the record and applicable law, we conclude that Metro Sewer and Metro

Government are entitled to summary judgment because Lampton’s claims are not

ripe.

 Under §§ 13 and 242 of the Kentucky Constitution and the Fifth

Amendment to the United States Constitution, “the government may not take a

citizen’s private property without providing just compensation.” Farmers Nat’l

Bank v. Commonwealth Dep’t of Revenue, 486 S.W.3d 872, 883 (Ky. App. 2015).

 -5-
 The classic version of a taking occurs when the government seizes property for its

own use. See, e.g., Palazzolo v. Rhode Island, 533 U.S. 606, 617 (2001) (“The

clearest sort of taking occurs when the government encroaches upon or occupies

private land for its own proposed use.”).

 However, there is another type of governmental taking variously

referred to as a reverse taking, an inverse taking, an inverse condemnation, or a

regulatory taking. “Inverse condemnation is the term applied to a suit against a

government to recover the fair market value of property which has in effect been

taken and appropriated by the activities of the government when no eminent

domain proceedings are used.” Commonwealth, Nat. Res. and Env’t Prot. Cabinet

v. Stearns Coal and Lumber Co., 678 S.W.2d 378, 381 (Ky. 1984). As the United

States Supreme Court has described it, “there will be instances when government

actions do not encroach upon or occupy the property yet still affect and limit its use

to such an extent that a taking occurs” because the applicable governmental

regulation “goes too far. . . .” Palazzolo, 533 U.S. at 617 (internal quotation marks

and citations omitted). A governmental regulation “goes too far” when it “denies

all economically beneficial or productive use of land. . . .” Id. (internal quotation

marks and citations omitted). That is what Lampton asserts occurred here.

 But “[a] court cannot determine whether a regulation has gone ‘too

far’ unless it knows how far the regulation goes.” MacDonald, Sommer & Frates

 -6-
 v. Yolo Cnty., 477 U.S. 340, 348 (1986). Thus, as the Supreme Court has

explained:

 a takings claim based on a law or regulation which is
 alleged to go too far in burdening property depends upon
 the landowner’s first having followed reasonable and
 necessary steps to allow regulatory agencies to exercise
 their full discretion in considering development plans for
 the property, including the opportunity to grant any
 variances or waivers allowed by law. As a general rule,
 until these ordinary processes have been followed the
 extent of the restriction on property is not known and a
 regulatory taking has not yet been established.

Palazzolo, 533 U.S. at 620–21. The Supreme Court further stated that “[u]ntil a

property owner has obtained a final decision regarding the application of the

zoning ordinance and subdivision regulations to its property, it is impossible to tell

whether the land retain[s] any reasonable beneficial use or whether [existing]

expectation interests ha[ve] been destroyed.” Yolo County, 477 U.S. at 349.

(internal quotation marks and citations omitted).

 The Supreme Court has explained that a case is not ripe until a “final

decision” has been made because the entities who enforce local land-use policies

possess a “high degree of discretion” to grant exceptions to those policies, so “a

sound judgment about what use will be allowed simply cannot be made by asking

whether a parcel’s characteristics or a proposal’s details facially conform to the

terms of the general use regulations.” Suitum v. Tahoe Reg’l Plan. Agency, 520

U.S. 725, 739 (1997). In plain English, a takings claim is not ripe “if avenues still

 -7-
 remain for the government to clarify or change its decision.” Pakdel v. City and

Cnty. of San Francisco, California, 594 U.S. 474, 480 (2021).

 Although those Supreme Court decisions were based on federal law

and the United States Constitution, the same general ripeness principles apply

under Kentucky law. For example, our Supreme Court applied ripeness principles

to a reverse condemnation claim brought under Kentucky law in Spanish Cove

Sanitation, Inc. v. Louisville-Jefferson County Metropolitan Sewer District, 72

S.W.3d 918 (Ky. 2002). In Spanish Cove Sanitation, the owner of a wastewater

treatment facility filed a reverse condemnation action when Metro Sewer had

merely “planned to tie into the pipe system that served [the wastewater treatment

facility’s] customers.” Id. at 919. In other words, the plaintiff filed suit based on

only a plan, without Metro Sewer having actually “tied into” the plaintiff’s sewer

lines. Id.

 Our Supreme Court held the suit was not ripe:

 At the outset, we should note that the trial court
 did not abuse its discretion in determining that the issue
 was not ripe. Under Kentucky law, before a plaintiff can
 make a claim of inverse condemnation, there must be an
 actual taking. Holloway Const. Co. v. Smith, Ky., 683
 S.W.2d 248, 249 (1984). In Associated Industries of
 Kentucky v. Commonwealth, Ky., 912 S.W.2d 947
 (1995), we held that Kentucky courts cannot grant
 advisory opinions or rule on hypothetical questions, but
 rather must rule on real disputes. At the time this action
 was filed, nothing had even arguably been taken.

leads.caseName: K & L CRYSTAL BEACH, LLC, and ROBERT E. BOHMAN v. THE CRYSTAL BEACH CONDOMINIUM ASSOCIATION, INC., an Idaho Non-Profit Corporation; MARVIN ASKEY, ROBERT SCHWENKFELDER, EDWARD BARRETT, CHRISTOPHER BRAZIL, RONALD GROVE, MICHAEL VIRDEN, MARY MARTIN, PATTI ZATICA, TYLER BUTTERFIELD, DARRELL CARNEY, JOHN DOES 1-60 AND JANE DOES 1-60, Encroachers
leads.text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF THE STATE OF IDAHO
 Docket No. 52887

 K & L CRYSTAL BEACH, LLC, and )
 ROBERT E. BOHMAN, )
 )
 Plaintiffs-Appellants, )
 )
 v. )
 )
 THE CRYSTAL BEACH CONDOMINIUM ) Boise, August 2026 Term
 ASSOCIATION, INC., an Idaho non-profit )
 corporation; MARVIN ASKEY, ROBERT ) Opinion Filed: October 30, 2026
 SCHWENKFELDER, EDWARD BARRETT, )
 CHRISTOPHER BRAZIL, RONALD ) Melanie Gagnepain, Clerk
 GROVE, MICHAEL VIRDEN, MARY )
 MARTIN, PATTI ZATICA, TYLER )
 BUTTERFIELD, DARRELL CARNEY, )
 JOHN DOES 1-60 AND JANE DOES 1-60, )
 Encroachers, )
 )
 Defendants-Respondents. )

 Appeal from the District Court of the Fourth Judicial District, State of Idaho, Valley
 County. Jason D. Scott, District Judge.

 The decision of the district court is affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded.

 Wright Brothers Law Office, Twin Falls, for Appellants. Brooke B. Redmond
 argued.

 Eberle, Berlin, Kading, Turnbow & McKlveen Chartered, Boise, for Respondents.
 Evan M. Westerfield argued.

 _____________________

MEYER, Justice.
 The Crystal Beach Condominium Association, Inc., (“CBCA”) is an Idaho non-profit
corporation serving as the owners’ association for the Crystal Beach Condominiums in McCall,
Idaho. In 2020, CBCA recorded an amended condominium declaration that altered the allocation
of owners’ common area interests and assessments, along with new rental rules and moorage rules.
Two unit owners in the complex, K & L Crystal Beach, LLC, and Robert E. Bohman (collectively,
“K&L”), filed suit against CBCA and former members of CBCA’s board of directors (collectively
 “the Association”). K&L alleged claims for declaratory relief, slander of title, quiet title,
encroachment, and breach of contract, which were premised on K&L’s contention that the
Association unlawfully changed K&L’s ownership and rental rights under Idaho law or under the
Association’s declaration. K&L also filed a claim seeking to compel the Association to remeasure
unit square footage and reallocate ownership interests pursuant to Idaho Code section 55-
1505(1)(c) of the Condominium Property Act.
 The district court granted summary judgment on K&L’s claims in favor of the Association,
concluding that K&L’s first five claims were barred because K&L failed to satisfy the statutory
requirements for bringing derivative claims under Idaho’s Nonprofit Corporation Act. The court
also concluded that K&L failed to establish that the Association acted in bad faith when it
reallocated ownership interests in 2020; therefore, K&L was not entitled to specific performance.
 On appeal, K&L contends the district court erroneously granted summary judgment on its
first five claims because (1) Idaho’s Condominium Property Act, not the Nonprofit Corporation
Act, governed its claims and expressly grants unit owners “standing and authority” to enforce the
declaration and bylaws under Idaho Code section 55-1516; (2) even if the Nonprofit Corporation
Act governed, its claims were not derivative because the individualized harm to K&L’s property
interests were independent of its membership status. K&L also argued that the district court erred
in dismissing its claim seeking to remeasure and reallocate ownership interests under section 55-
1505(1)(c) because the question of bad faith was a disputed issue of material fact. For the reasons
set forth below, we affirm in part, reverse in part, and remand.
 I. FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND
 A. Factual Background
 In October 1971, CBCA was organized as an Idaho non-profit corporation for a waterfront
condominium complex located in McCall, Idaho. About a month later, the Association recorded
the Condominium Declaration for the Crystal Beach Condominiums (the “Original Declaration”).
“A declaration is essentially a master deed which defines the rights and duties of the developer,
the owners of the individual condominium units and the management body of the project.”
Thompson v. Ebbert, 144 Idaho 315, 317, 160 P.3d 754, 756 (2007) (citation modified). Pertinent
to this appeal, the Original Declaration provides in Article XIV that amendments to the Original
Declaration require the consent of owners representing an aggregate ownership interest of 85%
and “all holders of any recorded Mortgage covering or affecting any or all of the Condominiums”:
  This Declaration shall not be revoked nor shall any of the provisions herein
 be amended unless the Owners representing an aggregate ownership interest of 85%
 or more of the Condominiums, as reflected on the real estate records of Valley
 County, Idaho, and all holders of any recorded Mortgage covering or affecting any
 or all of the Condominiums, whose interests as Mortgagees appear in such records,
 consent and agree to such revocation or amendment by instruments duly recorded.
 Any such revocation or amendment shall be binding upon every Owner and every
 Condominium whether the burdens thereon are increased or decreased by any such
 amendment and whether the Owner of each and every Condominium consents
 thereto.
 Article XVI, section 16.1 of the Original Declaration provides “the Association on behalf
of the Owners, or, in a proper case, by an aggrieved Owner” may maintain “an action to recover
sums due and damages or injunctive relief” when an owner fails to comply with the Association’s
declaration or by-laws:
 Each Owner shall comply with the provisions of this Declaration, the Articles of
 Incorporation and the By-Laws of the Association, and the decisions and
 resolutions of the Association adopted pursuant thereto as the same may be lawfully
 amended from time to time. Failure to comply with any of the same shall be grounds
 for an action to recover sums due and damages or injunctive relief or both,
 maintainable by the Association on behalf of the Owners, or, in a proper case, by
 an aggrieved Owner.
Lastly, Article X, section 10.1 provides that the units may be leased or rented.
 Bohman and K&L Crystal Beach, LLC, each own a unit in the complex. “[C]ondominium
ownership is a hybrid form of interest in real property, entitling an owner to (1) fee simple
ownership of a unit and (2) an undivided interest in common with the other unit owners in the
common areas.” McLaughlin v. Moore, 176 Idaho 726, ___, 582 P.3d 11, 20 (2025) (citing I.C. §§
55-1503(a), 55-101B). Under the Original Declaration, each unit carries a 1.595% common-area
ownership and voting share, for a combined allocation of 3.19%. Kathleen Glover is the sole
member of K&L Crystal Beach. Defendants Marvin Askey, Robert Schwenkfelder, Edward
Barrett, Christopher Brazil, Ronald Grove, Michael Virden, Mary Martin, Patti Zattica, Tyler
Butterfield, and Darrell Carney are past members of the CBCA’s board of directors (the “Board”).
 In 1993, Marvin Askey purchased a two-bedroom “loft” unit with a balcony area that “had
been enclosed by exterior doors” and an attic space that “is only accessible from within” the unit.
In 2013, Askey remodeled his unit, with the Board’s approval, by adding a vaulted ceiling in one
bedroom.
 In May 2018, Bohman sent a letter to the Board raising concerns that members had
encroached on common or limited common areas while remodeling attic and patio spaces.
 Thereafter, the Board held several meetings to discuss the alleged encroachments, and, on August
21, 2018, it approved an audit of three buildings in the complex by architect Cathy Sewell.
However, according to Glover’s declaration submitted in opposition to summary judgment, Askey
voted against the audit, and “[t]he then president of the board Patty Ely, never signed the agreement
with Cathy Sewell to allow her to do the work.”
 In December 2018, the Board received advice of its attorney, Amy Pemberton, regarding
the encroachment issue and whether a member’s remodeling would require the Board to
recalculate the ownership percentages under Idaho Code section 55-1505(1)(c). Pemberton opined
that (1) a recalculation would only be required if the unit’s useable square footage was expanded
beyond its original boundaries, and (2) that any unit that added cubic space beyond the original
boundaries during a remodel would constitute an encroachment into the general common area. She
further stated that “finishing off a loft to be livable space would increase the square footage of the
[u]nit” and advised the Board on the procedure for amending its governing documents to
accommodate a reallocation of the owner’s interest in the common area. According to Glover, “the
board president, now Robert Schwankfelder, did not sign the agreement with Cathy Sewell
allowing her to measure the units and resolve the square footage issues.” Thereafter, the Board did
not move forward with Sewell’s audit.
 In January 2020, the Board provided its members with six options for amending the
provisions of the Original Declaration, which addressed, among other things, a reallocation of
owner’s interests in common areas and liability for assessments. Pertinent here, “Option #5”
allocated ownership interests “according to relative square footage, and voting and assessments as
they are today.” Owners representing an aggregate ownership interest of 88.33% consented to
adopting Option 5. About two weeks later, the Board recorded an Amended and Restated
Declaration for the Crystal Beach Condominiums (the “Amended Declaration”). Notably, while
the Original Declaration allocated each of K&L’s units a 1.595% of undivided interest in the
common area, the Amended Declaration allocated each unit a 1.397% “Percentage Ownership [i]n
Common Area” and 1.595% “Assessment Allocation Percentage.”
 After the Amended Declaration was recorded, Craig Marcus, a mortgagee, sent a letter to
the Board stating that its recording of the Amended Declaration did not comport with Article XIV
of the Original Declaration, which required the consent of all mortgagees. Thereafter, Marcus
recorded a “Mortgagee’s Notice of Refusal to Consent or Agree to Amendment[.]” In his notice,
 Marcus stated that his recorded consent was required to approve amendments to the Original
Declaration under Article XIV and that he did not consent.
 In February 2020, the Board disseminated rental rules governing owners’ rights to rent
their units. These rules are not in the record, and their contents are unknown. According to a
declaration submitted by Glover in opposition to summary judgment, the Board “threatened fines
or evictions if people failed to comply with the rules and regulations.” In response, Glover sent a
letter to the Board alleging that the proposed rules violated former Idaho Code section 55-115,
which prohibited “homeowner’s association[s]” from enforcing restrictions that limit “the
rental . . . of any property, land or structure thereon within the jurisdiction of the homeowner’s
association, unless expressly agreed to in writing at the time of such addition or amendment by the
owner of the affected property.” I.C. § 55-115(3) (2020). Bohman also objected to the rental rules,
stating that he would not consent and that they violated section 55-115(3) (2020). The record does
not clarify what actions, if any, the Board took on the 2020 rules.
 In 2022, the Board again disseminated rental rules along with amendments to its moorage
rules. It is unclear whether these rules were the same rules disseminated by the Board in 2020. The
rental rules included, among other things, limits on pets and maximum occupancy and that renters’
guests could not “utilize the common areas” or “stay in the units overnight.” The moorage rules
provided in part that vessels must be titled in the name of the unit owner or the owner’s children,
and that the transfer of a unit’s ownership during an estate administration to an adult child would
not affect moorage license priority. Thereafter, Glover sent a letter to the Board, again claiming
that the rental rules violated Idaho Code section 55-115(3) (2020) (the law was recodified as Idaho
Code section 55-3211 as of July 1, 2022). She further

leads.text:
Nebraska Supreme Court Online Library
www.nebraska.gov/apps-courts-epub/
10/30/2026 08:18 AM CDT

 - 710 -
 Nebraska Supreme Court Advance Sheets
 322 Nebraska Reports
 11819 MIRACLE HILLS DRIVE v. ALI
 Cite as 322 Neb. 710

 11819 Miracle Hills Drive, LP, appellee, v.
 Maman Lawan Ali, appellant.
 ___ N.W.3d ___

 Filed October 30, 2026. No. S-25-461.

 1. Summary Judgment: Appeal and Error. An appellate court reviews
 the district court’s grant of summary judgment de novo, viewing the
 record in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party and drawing

 (Reissue 2016) must be filed with the district court.

 Appeal from the District Court for Douglas County: Katie L.
 Benson, Judge. Vacated and remanded for further proceedings.

 Chinedu Igbokwe, of Banwo & Igbokwe Law Firm, L.L.C.,

 Funke, C.J., Cassel, Stacy, Papik, Freudenberg,
Bergevin, and Vaughn, JJ.
 Bergevin, J.
 INTRODUCTION
 Maman Lawan Ali appeals from the district court’s decree
foreclosing his interest in his marital residence, which he owns
with his wife as a joint tenant with right of survivorship. The
decree ordered “the Sheriff or a special master of Plaintiff’s
choice” to sell the real property to satisfy a judgment lien that
11819 Miracle Hills Drive, LP (Miracle Hills), obtained against
Ali individually. The primary issue before us is the applicabil-
ity and operation of the homestead statutes 1 to the facts of
this case. We conclude that the homestead exemption did not
prevent the court from entering the decree. However, we find
plain error in the decree and, accordingly, vacate the decree
and remand the cause for further proceedings.
 BACKGROUND
 In a prior action, Miracle Hills obtained a money judgment
against Ali related to a commercial lease agreement. Miracle
Hills filed the instant action by way of a “Complaint for
Foreclosure of Judgment Lien (Equity),” seeking to foreclose
its judgment lien against Ali’s undivided one-half interest in
real property owned by him and his wife as joint tenants with
rights of survivorship. It is undisputed that the property is the
couple’s primary residence and family home. In their answers
to Miracle Hills’ complaint, neither Ali nor his wife raised
any defenses or counterclaims.
 Miracle Hills moved for summary judgment. At the hear-
ing on the motion, Ali and his wife appeared, both self-
represented. Three exhibits were offered and received. The

first exhibit was an affidavit from Miracle Hills’ property man-
ager and business records manager. The affidavit set forth that
Miracle Hills obtained a judgment against Ali for his breach
of a commercial lease agreement and attached a certified copy
of the judgment. The second exhibit was a stipulation between
Miracle Hills and the real property’s mortgagee setting forth
that the mortgagee’s interest in the property was senior to
Miracle Hills’. The third exhibit was a copy of the commercial
lease agreement, which showed that Ali’s wife was not a party
to the lease.
 Ali argued that the property “is my residential house with
my family, [where] I live with my four children and my wife.
And I don’t see legally . . . how my house can be foreclosed.”
However, he was unable to cite to any law in support of his
argument. His wife argued that the judgment was against Ali
alone and that “the ownership of the house is protected by
the Nebraska law.” She maintained that the “house cannot be
foreclosed because the interest is for both of us, and they don’t
have [a] judgment against myself.” She contended that (1) a
judgment lien cannot attach to a nondebtor property interest
and (2) her ownership interest is protected by tenancy in the
entirety, as such property cannot be subject to a judgment lien
against only one spouse; thus, Miracle Hills could not divide
her and Ali’s interest by foreclosure.
 In its decree, the district court found that there were no
issues of fact and that Ali and his wife did not set forth any
valid defenses in their answers. The court found that Miracle
Hills had a judgment lien based on the prior judgment and
that its lien was second in priority to the mortgagee’s deed
of trust.
 The court ordered that unless the debt was paid in full
within 20 days, “the Sheriff or a special master of [Miracle
Hills’] choice, shall, . . . sell the Real Property and appur-
tenances [and] bring the proceeds of the sale into Court to
be applied to the satisfaction of the sums so found due upon
confirmation of said sale.” The definition of “Real Property”

 Ali filed a timely appeal.
 ASSIGNMENTS OF ERROR
 Ali assigns that the trial court erred in (1) granting sum-
mary judgment despite material issues of fact regarding the
homestead status of the property, (2) ordering foreclosure
of his undivided interest in the marital residence contrary to
§§ 40-101 and 40-103, and (3) extending a judgment lien
against one spouse to divest the nondebtor spouse of her co-
ownership interest in the homestead.
 STANDARD OF REVIEW
 [1,2] An appellate court reviews the district court’s grant
of summary judgment de novo, viewing the record in the
light most favorable to the nonmoving party and drawing all
reasonable inferences in that party’s favor. 2 A grant of sum-
mary judgment will be affirmed if the pleadings and admitted
evidence show that there is no genuine issue as to any material
facts or as to the ultimate inferences that may be drawn from
the facts and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as
a matter of law. 3
 [3] When an appeal calls for statutory interpretation or pres-
ents questions of law, an appellate court must reach an inde-
pendent, correct conclusion irrespective of the determination
made by the court below. 4
2
 Schuemann v. Timperley, 321 Neb. 955, 38 N.W.3d 417 (2026).
3
 Id.
4
 Park ‘N Go v. Airport Authority, 321 Neb. 798, 37 N.W.3d 459 (2026).
 See Chambers v. Bringenberg, 309 Neb. 888, 963 N.W.2d 37 (2021).

 ANALYSIS
 We begin by recognizing the unique action that Miracle
Hills brought to enforce its judgment lien. Instead of seeking
a writ of execution on Ali’s property, 5 Miracle Hills brought
what it called an equitable foreclosure action. We have, at
least on two occasions, recognized such an action; however,
the facts of those cases were extreme and readily distinguish-
able from the instant action. 6 Nevertheless, the district court
heard the action and entered a decree, and Ali has not chal-
lenged the type of action brought. Accordingly, we do not con-
sider whether an equitable foreclosure action is proper under
these circumstances.
 On appeal, all three of Ali’s assignments of error concern
the effect and applicability of the homestead exemption to this
case. In sum, he argues that the homestead exemption pre-
vented the district court from ordering the sale of his interest
in the real property. Miracle Hills argues that, if the homestead
exemption applies, it is not a defense to foreclosure but applies
“at the execution stage.” 7 As we discuss below, we disagree
with both parties. To understand why, we first provide an over-
view of the homestead statutes 8 before turning to the resolu-
tion of this case.
 Homestead Statutes
 We have explained that the purpose of the Legislature in
enacting the homestead statutes was to protect the debtor and
the debtor’s family residing in a home from the forced sale of
the home on execution or attachment. 9 A homestead is gener-
ally “exempt from judgment liens and from execution or forced

debts not exempted by the general rule, such as mechanics’

any event, “the homestead of a married person cannot be
conveyed or encumbered unless the instrument by which it is
conveyed or encumbered is executed . . . by both spouses.” 12
 A homestead has certain characteristics. In its inception,
a homestead is a parcel of land on which the family resides,
and which is to them a home. 13 It is specific to “[e]ach natu-
ral person,” requires the claimant to reside in “the dwelling
house,” and is “to be selected by the owner.” 14 A homestead is
constituted by the two acts of selection and residence. 15

leads.caseName: Veena Dental PA v. Brixmor GA Apollo II TX LP
leads.text:
NUMBER 13-26-00002-CV

 COURT OF APPEALS

 THIRTEENTH DISTRICT OF TEXAS

 CORPUS CHRISTI – EDINBURG

VEENA DENTAL PA, Appellant,

 v.

BRIXMOR GA APOLLO II TX LP, Appellee.

 ON APPEAL FROM THE 343RD DISTRICT COURT
 OF SAN PATRICIO COUNTY, TEXAS

 MEMORANDUM OPINION

 Before Chief Justice Tijerina and Justices Cron and Fonseca
 Memorandum Opinion by Justice Fonseca

 Appellant Veena Dental PA (Veena) appeals the trial court’s grant of appellee

Brixmor GA Apollo II TX LP’s (Brixmor) traditional motion for summary judgment. Veena

argues it presented competent summary judgment evidence raising a genuine issue of

material fact regarding its claims. We affirm because the record conclusively shows

Veena’s claims are barred by limitations.
  I. BACKGROUND

 On March 23, 2013, Veena leased a property located at 1548 Wildcat Drive in

Portland (Premises) from Brixmor, a real estate entity, intending to rebuild and use the

Premises as a dental office. According to the lease, the Premises had “approximate

dimensions of 32 feet of frontage and 59 feet of depth, for an approximate total square

foot area of 1,863.” During email communications in 2013, the parties negotiated the price

per square foot of the Premises. The parties extended the lease in September 2018 via

amendment.

 The lease states in Section 16.01: “IN THE EVENT [Brixmor] TRANSFERS THIS

LEASE, [Brixmor] WILL BE RELEASED FROM ALL LIABILITY AND OBLIGATIONS

HEREUNDER, PROVIDED THAT THE TRANSFEREE ASSUMES THE OBLIGATIONS

OF THIS LEASE.” Section 16.05 states all “liabilities and obligations” are assigned to the

new owner in the event Brixmor sold the Premises. The lease also contained a waiver of

Texas Deceptive Trade Practice Act (DTPA) claims and limits recovery for any default or

breach by Brixmor “TO THE ESTATE AND PROPERTY OF [Brixmor] IN THE LAND AND

BUILDING.” The lease further contained a clause that the property was delivered in “AS-

IS/WHERE-IS” condition. In November 2018, Brixmor sold the Northshore Plaza

shopping center, of which the Premises was part, to Northshore Plaza LP (Northshore).

Brixmor assigned Veena’s lease to Northshore and Northshore assumed Brixmor’s

obligations pursuant to the lease.

 In 2023, Veena discovered the area of the Premises was in fact about 1,500 square

feet after taking measurements of the space. Veena also asserted the correct dimensions

were reflected in “the construction plans for the buildout of the” Premises, which were

 2
 drawn on March 13, 2013, and showed a “Finish-Out SQ. FT” of 1,432. Upon discovery

of this discrepancy, Veena demanded reimbursement for alleged rent “overpayments”

and future rent reduction, but Brixmor refused to comply.

 Veena filed suit on May 22, 2024, asserting claims for breach of contract, fraud,

and DTPA violations, and seeking “damages that are within the jurisdictional limits of the

court,” attorney’s fees, and costs. Veena contended Brixmor deliberately mispresented

the actual size of the Premises, charging more rent in accordance with this

misrepresented size. Brixmor filed its answer making a general denial and asserting it

was not liable because it sold the Premises to a successor landlord in 2018. Brixmor also

asserted defenses of estoppel, waiver, release, statutes of limitations, “as-is” clauses in

the lease, and laches, among other defenses. The parties conducted discovery in August

2025, and Veena admitted in interrogatories that Northshore took over as landlord in

2018. Veena also admitted its construction plans reflected the true size of the Premises.

 On August 15, 2025, Brixmor filed its traditional motion for summary judgment

arguing limitations had run on Veena’s claims and that it was the wrong party to sue as it

sold the property back in 2018. Brixmor asserted that Northstar assumed all obligations

under the lease in 2018 and Brixmor had no contact with Veena afterwards. Brixmor

further argued Veena’s claims accrued in 2013 when the parties entered into the lease or

when Veena took possession of the Premises. Thus, Brixmor asserted limitations ran on

all of Veena’s claims in 2015 or 2017. Brixmor further claimed Veena did not plead the

discovery rule, but even if it had, discovery indicated Veena had possession of

construction plans reflecting the true dimensions since it occupied the Premises and likely

reviewed those plans before commencing construction. Brixmor also argued Veena

 3
 already collected for overpaid rent from Northstar.

 Veena responded to the motion arguing genuine issues of material fact existed as

to each of its claims. Specifically, Veena asserted the discovery rule tolled limitations

because it could not have discovered the true size of the space because it had no reason

to measure the space and did not have “comparable knowledge of what a 1,500 square

foot space looked like.” It claimed to discover the discrepancy only by accident. Veena

further argued there were genuine issues of material fact as to the breach of contract,

fraud, and DTPA claims because Brixmor made material misrepresentations and claimed

the construction plans did not reflect the square footage. Veena attached a copy of the

construction plans to its response. Veena did not file an amended petition asserting the

discovery rule.

 The trial court set the traditional motion for summary judgment for submission by

briefs on September 22, 2025. On September 30, 2025, the trial court signed an order

granting Brixmor’s motion and entered a final judgment. Veena filed a motion for

reconsideration and motion for new trial. Brixmor responded to this motion, arguing Veena

failed to assert any fact the trial court erred on and asserting the discovery rule could not

be considered because Veena failed to amend its petition to affirmatively plead that

defensive theory. Brixmor also argued the plans attached to Veena’s response contained

the Premises’ dimensions and were dated 2013, meaning the size was reasonably

discoverable prior entering the lease.

 The trial court denied Veena’s motion for reconsideration on November 18, 2025.

This appeal followed.

 4
  II. ANALYSIS

 Veena’s sole issue challenges the trial court’s grant of summary judgment.

A. Standard of Review

 “We review a summary judgment ruling de novo.” H-E-B, LP v. Peterson, 732

S.W.3d 541, 545 (Tex. 2026). “We view evidence ‘in the light most favorable to the

nonmovant, indulging every reasonable inference and resolving any doubts against the

motion.’” Id. (quoting City of Keller v. Wilson, 168 S.W.3d 802, 824 (Tex. 2005)). A movant

for traditional summary judgment has the burden to establish that no genuine issue of

material fact exists and that it is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. TEX. R. CIV. P.

166a(a)(1). If the movant meets its burden, the burden shifts to the non-movant to raise

a genuine issue of material fact precluding summary judgment. Lujan v. Navistar, Inc.,

555 S.W.3d 79, 84 (Tex. 2018). If the nonmovant provides more than a scintilla of

evidence to raise a fact issue, then summary judgment is improper. San Patricio Cnty.

Appraisal Dist. v. Gunvor USA LLC, 731 S.W.3d 908, 917 (Tex. App.—Corpus Christi–

Edinburg 2026, pet. granted); Cardenas v. Bilfinger TEPSCO, Inc., 527 S.W.3d 391, 398

(Tex. App.—Houston [1st Dist.] 2017, no pet.). A scintilla is enough evidence to rise to a

level where reasonable and fair-minded people could differ in their conclusions whereas

less than a scintilla creates no more than a mere surmise or suspicion. See Gunvor USA

LLC, 731 S.W.3d at 917; Cardenas, 527 S.W.3d at 398.

B. Statute of Limitations

 One of the grounds the trial court granted summary judgment on was Brixmor’s

affirmative defense of statute of limitations. “A summary judgment granted on the basis

of an affirmative defense will be affirmed only if the record establishes that the movant

 5
 conclusively proved all elements of its affirmative defense as a matter of law.” Deacero,

S.A.P.I. de C.V. v. BNSF Ry. Co., 696 S.W.3d 212, 217 (Tex. App.—Houston [14th Dist.]

2024, pet. granted) (citing City of Houston v. Clear Creek Basin Auth., 589 S.W.2d 671,

678 (Tex. 1979)). “To obtain summary judgment on limitations grounds, the movant must

conclusively establish the accrual date of the cause of action.” Eagle Oil & Gas Co. v.

TRO-X, L.P., 619 S.W.3d 699, 708 (Tex. 2021). A limitations period begins to accrue

when a wrongful act causes legal injury even if all damages have yet to occur. Id. at 707–

08 (quoting S.V. v. R.V., 933 S.W.2d 1, 4 (Tex. 1996)).

 Veena brought causes of action for breach of contract 1 and fraud, which are both

subject to a four-year statute of limitations, and DTPA claims, which are subject to a two-

year statute of limitations. See TEX. CIV. PRAC. & REM. CODE §§ 16.051, 16.004; TEX. BUS.

& COM. CODE § 17.565. A breach of contract claim accrues when the contract is breached.

Trinity Indus. Leasing Co. v. Lattimore Materials Corp., 736 S.W.3d 19, 26 (Tex. App.—

Dallas 2024, pet. granted). 2 For fraud, however, a claim does not accrue “until the plaintiff

discovers, or in the exercise of reasonable care and diligence should have discovered,

the fraud.” Harris v. Am. Prot. Ins., 158 S.W.3d 614, 628 (Tex. App.—Fort Worth 2005,

no pet.). Likewise, the limitations period for a DTPA claim begins when a plaintiff

 1 While Veena brought a claim for breach of contract, we note its claim is more properly

characterized as fraudulent inducement. “[F]raudulent inducement ‘is a particular species of fraud that
arises only in the context of a contract and requires the existence of a contract as part of its proof.’” Holloway
v. Dekkers, 380 S.W.3d 315, 324 (Tex. App.—Dallas 2012, no pet.) (quoting Haase v. Glazner, 62 S.W.3d
795, 798–99 (Tex. 2001)). The heart of such claim is that one party induced the other into executing a
contract through the use of fraudulent misrepresentations, as Veena alleges Brixmor did here. See id.
Neither party has raised this issue, so we proceed with the analysis based on the parties’ characterization
of the cause of action and the applicable law as it was presented.

 2 While, as we noted, Veena’s claim is better categorized as fraudulent inducement, we note the

statute of limitations is the same as for breach of contract: four years. See TEX. CIV. PRAC. & REM. CODE
§ 16.004(a)(4). A fraudulent inducement claim accrues on the date the allegedly false representations were
made, which on this record, is the same date Veena signed the contract if not earlier. See Seureau v.
ExxonMobil Corp., 274 S.W.3d 206, 227 (Tex. App.—Houston [14th Dist.] 2008, no pet.).

 6
 discovers “or in the exercise of reasonable diligence should have discovered” the

offending act. TEX. BUS. & COM. CODE § 17.565.

 Here, the wrongful act causing legal injury was Brixmor’s alleged

misrepresentation regarding the Premises’ footage inducing Veena to sign the lease.

Veena signed the lease with Brixmor on March 23, 2013, thus beginning its obligations to

pay rent and its legal injury of being allegedly overcharged. See Eagle Oil & Gas Co., 619

S.W.3d at 707–08. Therefore, Brixmor has conclusively established the accrual date of

Veena’s breach of contract cause of action was March 23, 2013. See id.; Deacero,

S.A.P.I. de C.V., 696 S.W.3d at 217; Stine v. Stewart, 80 S.W.3d 586, 592 (Tex. 2002).

Any action for breach of contract was required to be brought before March 23, 2017,

which Veena undisputedly failed to do.

 However, Veena argues the discovery rule in its brief. The discovery rule operates

akin to the accrual of limitations for fraud and DTPA violations in that it prevents the

statute of limitations from running “until the claimant knew or should have known of facts

that in the exercise of reasonable diligence would have led to the discovery of the wrongful

act.” Berry v. Berry, 646 S.W.3d 516, 524 (Tex. 2022) (quoting Little v. Smith, 943 S.W.2d

41

Court of Appeals 
Tenth Appellate District of Texas 

10-25-00196-CV 

Sandom Baumgardner, 
 Appellant 

v. 

Brazos River Authority, 
Appellee 

On appeal from the 
 170th District Court of McLennan County, Texas 
 Judge Jim Meyer, presiding 
Trial Court Cause No. 2017-3971-4 

JUSTICE HARRIS delivered the opinion of the Court. 

MEMORANDUM OPINION 

 In five points of error, Appellant Sandom Baumgardner contends that 
the trial court erred in granting judgment for Appellee Brazos River 
Authority (the “BRA”) on each of Baumgardner’s and the BRA’s claims for 
relief. In his first point of error, Baumgardner argues that the BRA’s denials 
of his permits to construct a concrete boat entryway and on-water boat dock 
for the benefit of his property were arbitrary and capricious. Relatedly, in his 

Baumgardner v. Brazos River Authority Page 2 

fourth and fifth points of error, Baumgardner asserts that the trial court 
erred in entering judgment for the BRA on its trespass and breach of 
restrictive covenant claims because the BRA’s denials of his permit 
applications were arbitrary and capricious. Finally, in his second and third 
points of error, Baumgardner argues that the trial court lacked jurisdiction to 
enter an injunction requiring Baumgardner to remove his improvements and 
that, even if the trial court had jurisdiction, injunctive relief is not proper in 
this case. We affirm. 
I. FACTUAL BACKGROUND AND 
PROCEDURAL HISTORY 

A. Factual Background 
Appellee Brazos River Authority is a political subdivision of the State of 
Texas established as a conservation and reclamation district under Article 
XVI, Section 59 of the Texas Constitution. Baumgardner v. Brazos River 
Auth., 714 S.W.3d 597, 600, 603 (Tex. 2025). The BRA was established in 
1929 for the purpose of managing portions of the watershed of the Brazos 
River. Id. at 600. 
In 1941, the BRA completed construction of the Morris Sheppard Dam, 
which impounded water up to 1000 feet above mean sea level—known as the 
“1000’ contour line”—to create Possum Kingdom Lake (the “Lake”). The BRA 
has owned all of the property beneath the 1000’ contour line since the BRA 

Baumgardner v. Brazos River Authority Page 3 

created the Lake. Additionally, prior to 2009, the BRA owned certain lots 
adjacent to the Lake above the 1000’ contour line. The BRA leased many of 
these lots to both residential and commercial occupants. By 2009, there were 
approximately 1,500 residential leased lots at the Lake owned by the BRA. 
In 2009, the Texas Legislature passed HB 3031, codified as T EX. SPEC. 
DIST. CODE § 8502.020 , requiring t he BRA to divest itself of, among other 
property, its “Leased Tract, ” comprising several lots that the BRA leased 
prior to 2009. TEX. SPEC. DIST. CODE § 8502.020(b )-(c). The Legislature 
further required the BRA to encumber the lots sold with certain enumerated 
restrictive covenants. TEX. SPEC. DIST. CODE § 8502.020(d). 
The BRA sold all of the roughly 1,500 leased lots to Patterson PK Land 
Partnership in October of 2010. The special warranty deed delivered to 
Patterson excluded from the conveyance all property beneath the 1000’ 
contour line, leaving that property under the BRA’s ownership. The deed 
further specified that Patterson took the property subject to certain deed 
restrictions—including those required by HB 3031—listed in a Declaration of 
Restrictive Covenants, Easements, and Conditions filed by the BRA in the 
official public records of Palo Pinto County, Texas. The Declaration provided 
that divested lots were subject to the BRA’s Shoreline Management Plan, a 

Baumgardner v. Brazos River Authority Page 4 

document created by the BRA in 2006 to manage and restrict the use of 
property adjacent to the Lake. 
Patterson subsequently sold various lots in the Leased Tract, including 
Lot 11, Area 12, District Tract 32- 1-48, the lot at issue in this suit. 
Baumgardner is the current owner of Lot 11, Area 12, District Tract 32- 1-48. 
Baumgardner acquired the property from the estate of Elton Bridges, who 
had acquired the property from Patterson. Both Bridges’ s and 
Baumgardner’s recorded deeds provide that the Lot is subject to the 
restrictions in the Declaration. Baumgardner further testified at trial that he 
received a copy of the Shoreline Management Plan when he purchased the 
property from Bridges. 
At the time Baumgardner acquired the property, it contained a house 
as well as a dock and adjoin ing walkway for the benefit of his property.
1 The 
Shoreline Management Plan prohibited the construction of additional 
improvements beneath the 1000’ contour line or on the surface of the Lake 
without prior approval from the BRA. 
In 2014, Baumgardner sought to dredge the property located beneath 
the 1000’ contour line but above the shoreline of the Lake, which w as over 
200 feet beneath Baumgardner’s dock at the time. Further, Baumgardner 

1 These structures are not at issue in this suit. 

Baumgardner v. Brazos River Authority Page 5 

sought to construct a “concrete boat entry way,” 2 purportedly for “erosion 
control.” Baumgardner contacted Kent Edwards, an inspection supervisor for 
the BRA at the Lake, who informed Baumgardner that the BRA could not 
grant him a permit for the boat entryway. Baumgardner claims here that 
Edwards also informed him that he would need a permit from the U.S. Army 
Corps of Engineers prior to completing any dredging work. Baumgardner 
received approval from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to complete the 
work on September 10, 2014. 
Four days later, Baumgardner submitted an application to the BRA for 
a permit to complete the dredging work and construct the boat entryway. 
The BRA responded by email, approving Baumgardner’s dredging work but 
denying him permission to construct the concrete boat entryway. As grounds 
for its denial, the BRA cited Section 3.7 of the Shoreline Management Plan, 
which prohibits the construction of new privately-held boat ramps on “leased 
lots.”
3 

2 We will refer to the concrete boat entryway as either the “boat entryway” or the “boat ramp” 
throughout this opinion. 

3 In October of 2014, the BRA amended the Regulations applicable to properties at the Lake to, in 
part, provide that “[n]ew privately held boat ramps and rail systems [were] no longer authorized for 
installation” on properties subject to the Regulations. The parties dispute whether, prior to this 
amendment, Baumgardner raised the issue that Section 3.7 only applied to “leased lots,” which 
Baumgardner apparently believed did not include his property. 

Baumgardner v. Brazos River Authority Page 6 

Baumgardner built the boat ramp anyway. Construction of the boat 
ramp, which was completed in April of 2015, was largely beneath the 1000’ 
contour line. In April and May of 2015, the BRA sent three letters to 
Baumgardner demanding that he remove the boat ramp. Baumgardner did 
not do so. Baumgardner also failed to remove the boat ramp after receiving 
demands from the BRA in November of 2016 and November of 2017, and the 
boat ramp remained on the BRA’s property at the time of trial of this cause in 
January of 2024. 
In October of 2017, Baumgardner submitted another application to the 
BRA, seeking a permit to modify his existing dock and adjoining walkway to 
attach a floating boat dock. 4 The BRA denied his application on the grounds 
that it would not consider granting him a permit until he had resolved the 
issues with the boat ramp. The BRA further threatened to revoke his permit 
for the existing on- water facilities on the grounds that Baumgardner was in 
default of the permit. 
Baumgardner installed the floating boat dock anyway. The BRA 
discovered the boat dock in March of 2020. On March 20, 2020, the BRA 
notified Baumgardner that his failure to remove the boat dock within 30 days 

4 Throughout this opinion, we will refer to the boat ramp and boat dock together as “the 
improvements.” 

Baumgardner v. Brazos River Authority Page 7 

would amount to a trespass and a violation of BRA regulations. 
Baumgardner did not remove the boat dock. 
B. Procedural History 
Baumgardner filed suit against the BRA in McLennan County District 
Court in November of 2017, seeking a declaration that the BRA could not 
require him to remove the boat ramp. The BRA removed the suit to the 
Western District of Texas, Waco Division, and that court remanded the suit 
back to the McLennan County District Court. Before remand, the BRA filed 
its answer and asserted counterclaims against Baumgardner for trespass, 
breach of restrictive covenant, and attorneys’ fees. 
Baumgardner subsequently amended his petition to assert a 
substantive due process claim against the BRA. Baumgardner alleged that 
the BRA’s denials of his permit applications were arbitrary and capricious 
and requested the court to order that his permit applications be approved. 
The BRA sustained its counterclaims through remand and requested an 
injunction ordering Baumgardner to remove the boat ramp and boat dock. 
The parties tried the case to a jury in January of 2024. The jury found 
that Baumgardner’s boat ramp and boat dock trespassed on the BRA’s 
property, that Baumgardner had breached the restrictive covenants by 
constructing the improvements, and that the BRA’s denials of Baumgardner’s 

Baumgardner v. Brazos River Authority Page 8 

permit applications were not arbitrary or capricious. After denying 
Baumgardner’s motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict, the trial 
court entered judgment in accordance with the jury verdicts. 
The trial court granted the BRA’s requested injunction. The final 
injunction required Baumgardner to remove the portion of the boat ramp 
beneath the 1000’ contour line and the entirety of the floating boat dock. 
Baumgardner appealed to this Court. After we determined that the 
case may fall under the Fifteenth Court of Appeals’s exclusive appellate 
jurisdiction, the Supreme Court of Texas transferred the appeal to the 
Fifteenth Court. The BRA moved to re -transfer the appeal to this Court, and 
the Fifteenth Court of Appeals forwarded the motion to the Texas Supreme 
Court. The Supreme Court issued an opinion, reported at Baumgardner v. 
Brazos River Authority, 714 S.W.3d 597 (Tex. 2025), in which it determined 
that the appeal did not fall within the Fifteenth Court’s exclusive 
jurisdiction. Accordingly, the Supreme Court transferred the case back to 
this Court. 
II. JURISDICTION 
Both parties make jurisdictional arguments on appeal. In response to 
Baumgardner’s first, fourth, and fifth points of error, the BRA argues that 
the trial court lacked jurisdiction to review the BRA’s decisions on 

Baumgardner v. Brazos River Authority Page 9 

Baumgardner’s permit applications. According to the BRA, it is entitled to 
immunity from suit, and neither this Court nor the trial court has 
jurisdiction to decide Baumgardner’s claims absent waiver or abrogation of 
immunity. 
In his third point of error, Baumgardner argues that the trial court 
erred in granting the BRA’s requested injunction because the injunction can 
only be awarded through successful pursuit of a forcible detainer action. 
Because the justice court has exclusive jurisdiction over forcible detainer 
actions, Baumgardner contends the trial court lacked jurisdiction to grant the 
injunction. We will address each of the preceding jurisdictional arguments in 
order. 
A. Governmental Immunity 
The BRA argues that governmental immunity deprived the trial court 
of jurisdiction to hear Baumgardner’s substantive due process claim. The 
BRA is entitled to governmental immunity, which makes it immune from 
both suit and liability. See Karl v. Brazos River Auth., 494 S.W.3d 168, 171 
(Tex. App.—Eastland 2015, pet. denied). Governmental immunity from suit 
divests Texas courts of jurisdiction to hear claims filed against a 
governmental unit absent waiver or abrogation of immunity. See State v

leads.caseName: Topilin v. Island House Tenant Corp.
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Topilin v Island House Tenant Corp. 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06396 
 October 29, 2026 
 Appellate Division, First Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Emile Topilin, Plaintiff-Appellant, 
 v 
 Island House Tenant Corp., et al., Defendants-Respondents. 

 Decided and Entered: October 29, 2026 
 Index No. 850655/23|Appeal No. 7397|Case No. 2024-07932| 
 Before: Renwick, P.J., Kennedy, Friedman, González, Chan, JJ. 

 David A. Kaminsky & Associates, P.C., New York (James A. English of counsel), for appellant. 
 Smith Buss & Jacobs LLP, New York (Jacqueline L. Aiello of counsel), for Island House Tenant Corp., respondent. 
 Falcon Rappaport & Berkman LLP, Rockville Centre (Michele K. Jaspan of counsel), for United Nations Federal Credit Union, respondent. 

 [*1] 
 Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Francis A. Kahn, III, J.), entered November 12, 2024, which, to the extent appealed from as limited by the briefs, granted the respective motions of defendants Island House Tenants Corp. and United Nations Federal Credit Union to dismiss the complaint, unanimously modified, on the law, to deny Island House Tenants Corp.'s motion as to the sixth cause of action for breach of the warranty of habitability, and otherwise affirmed, without costs. 
 The motion court properly dismissed plaintiff's claim for breach of the proprietary lease seeking an abatement of maintenance for the period his apartment was uninhabitable following a fire in his kitchen. Plaintiff acknowledged his failure to perform under the proprietary lease, negating an element of the claim ( see Harris v Seward Park Hous. Corp. , 79 AD3d 425, 426 [1st Dept 2010]). There is no dispute that the April 29, 2017 fire rendered the apartment untenantable; however, the motion court correctly determined that as a result of plaintiff's failure to procure property insurance as required under paragraph 3.2.5 of the proprietary lease, plaintiff was deemed to have (i) "irrevocably released" and (ii) "irrevocably agreed to indemnify and hold harmless" defendant Island House Tenants Corp. (the cooperative) "from any claim for damages" to the apartment and its contents "which, but for the Tenant-Shareholder's failure to obtain and maintain the required insurance coverage, would have been covered by insurance." Thus, the motion court properly found that plaintiff's election to withhold maintenance was a breach of his obligations under the proprietary lease, warranting denial of the related injunctive relief against the cooperative. 
 The second claim for breach of fiduciary duty was also properly dismissed, as plaintiff did not plead any "independent tortious acts" by the cooperative's board members with specificity ( see Peacock v Herald Sq. Loft Corp. , 67 AD3d 442, 442-443 [1st Dept 2009]; CPLR 3016[b]). Since no independent wrongful conduct by any particular board member was alleged, the cooperative's "decisions concerning the manner and extent of repairs and renovations to the building were within the scope of their authority under the by-laws and proprietary lease of the cooperative, and were therefore shielded from judicial review by the business judgment rule" ( Konrad v 136 E. 64th St. Corp. , 254 AD2d 110 [1st Dept 1998], lv dismissed 92 NY2d 1042 [1999]). Contrary to plaintiff's contention, the cooperative was entitled to seek the above-described release provided under paragraph 3.2.5 of the proprietary lease in connection with the repairs. 
 [*2] 
 Plaintiff's sixth cause of action for breach of the warranty of habitability should be reinstated.
